maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to-refer briefly to an event of very great national interest of which the cable has brought the news since our last meeting. I refer to the splendid achievement of a fellow-citizen of Toronto, Private W. J. Clifford, in winning the King's prize at the meeting of the National Rifle Association at Bisley. This, I need hardly mention, is the crowning honour of the great competition in marksmanship participated in annually by upwards of three thousand of the riflemen of the Empire, all the overseas dominions being well represented, tvhile the flower of the regular and volunteer forces of the mother country enter into the keenest competition for the honours of the meeting.
Private Clifford is of the Tenth Royal Grenadiers, a regiment that since rifle shooting has been in vogue as the pastime of the volunteers of Canada has been second to none in the distinctions it has achieved as a training school for marksmen. It is especially fitting, therefore, that the honour achieved by Private Clifford shall be shared by a regiment so generally recognized as worthy to bear it. It is the young rifleman's second visit to Bisley, but for several years Private Clifford has been conspicuous at the great Canadian meeting at Roekliffe, in 1909 for instance, winning one of the three prizes so generously offered by His Excellency, the Governor-General for competition here.
Besides winning the King's Prize, Private Clifford has won also, at Bisley this year, the Prince of Wales' prize for a competition entirely distinct, an achievement never before accomplished during the fifty years of the National Rifle Association competitions. Examination of the records shows that the same has figured only twice before since the very beginning, as the winner of these two prizes donated by royalty, but in each case the honour was achieved in separate years for each prize. Thus Sergt. Lawrence of the 1st Dumbarton won the Queen's Prize in 1882, and the Prince of Wales' Prize the following year; while Major Pollock won the Queen's in 1892 and the Prince of Wales' in 1896. It has remained for Private Clifford to set a new record for the new reign, and so to identify himself for all time with the generosity of His Majesty King George and Edward, Prince of Wales.
This is the third occasion, it is fitting for me to mention, that Canadian competitors at Bisley have brought distinction to their country as well as to themselves by winning the Queen's or the King's Prize. Hayhurst, already well-known as an Old Country rifle-
9998

man, led the way in 1895, shortly after he had come to Canada and joined the Thirteenth Regiment of Hamilton. Then Private
S.	J. Perry, a young Canadian of Vancouver, was the King's Prize winner in 1904; and Private Clifford is our third Gold Medallist.
Rifle shooting means much more to us as a nation than does any other sport. It is generally recognized as the mainspring of the interest in the training of many regiments, and it is the sole bond of communication between our volunteers in the several cities and provinces of Canada and between Canadians and their comrades in arms from over the seas. In addition rifle shooting is recognized as involving the best development of physical manhood and of character. No one but a good citizen, an exemplary man, can be successful as a marksman. The honour won by Private Clifford il specially worthy of recognition, and I therefore extend to him my congratulations and those of his friends in this country.

speakeroldname: Sir FREDERICK BORDEN (Minister of Militia and Defence).
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: I would ask the privilege, Mr. Speaker, as head of the Militia" Department, of saying-and I am sure I am expressing the opinion of all the members of the House-how much I am obliged to the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Russell) for having brought this matter up. All Canadians must be proud of the unprecedented performance of Private Clifford in having won not only the King's Prize but the Prince of Vv ales' prize in the same year. The shooting has been particularly good this year at Bisley. The Canadian team won among other prizes the McKinnon Cup, and tied with the British team for the Kolapore Cup, but unfortunately for the Canadians the British team made a greater number of marks at the longest range and therefore retained possession of the prize. It must be specially gratifying to know also that this good shooting has been made with a Canadian rifle, so that we have not only the best rifle probably in the world, but we have men who know how to use it.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext:
I am delighted to support the remarks so ably expressed by my good friend from Toronto (Mr. Russell) and by my friend the Minister of Militia. I may point out that the Grenadiers are not only splendid men on the ranges, but that on every occasion the Grenadier regiment of Toronto has had the opportunity of active service, the men have done credit to themselves and to the flag under which they fight. I may point out further, as an inducement to officers commanding regiments throughout the country, that not only are the Grenadiers to-day commanded by an officer, Col. Gooderham,
who takes the greatest interest in rifle shooting, but it has had the good fortune in times past to have had commanding officers who have devoted a great deal of attention to the science.
I might also state that Clifford, the winner of the King's prize, is greatly assisted by his wife, who encourages him to go to the front, and inspires him with _ courage to do well for his country; and his corps. Furthermore, the Grenadiers on the ranges are coached by the wife of the colonel of the regiment, "Mrs. Gooderham. In making these remarks, I desire, in the first place, to encourage officers commanding regiments to take greater interest in rifle shooting, and in the next place to point out that the wives and lady friends of the soldiers might perform a splendid service for the country by encouraging these young men in rifle shooting, as the ladies I have mentioned do. I cannot let this opportunity pass without saying a word for the officer commanding the Bisley team this year, and for the men composing that team, it was my privilege to see them at Bisley not long ago. Colonel Stimson, the commandant, was performing the work admirably, and he was fortunate in having with him his sisters, who rendered the lives of the soldiers in their quarters very pleasant by giving them every inducement to maintain the high spirit of Canadian manhood. The same characteristics are found in Major Burland, the adjutant of the team, and we were very fortunate in having an excellent coach in Mr. Richardson, who is well known to all our friends. I should not let this opportunity pass without supporting my good friend the Minister of Militia by saying a word for the weapon with which these prizes were won, namely, the Canadian Ross rifle. That rifle has established itself, not only in Canada, but in England, and in every country on the continent of Europe, and is to-day well known and appreciated. It is said that a prophet is not without honour except in his own country. The Ross rifle stands first among the serviceable rifles in the world to-day, and I would not be at all surprised, before many years roll^ around, to see the principles of the Ross rifle, with a different calibre and cartridge of course, adopted as the weapon of the British Empire. I might in justice to Clifford point out that one of the troubles of rifle shooting in hot weather is nickelling, and Clifford has invented a substance, which he gave to every man on the ranges, to prevent that; and his uniformly good shooting has probably been partly due to this invention of his own. I am sure that the House, and the country will join in congratulating Clifford and the Canadian team not only on their shooting, but on their splendid manly conduct.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in connection with this matter, the Minister of Militia might go a step further and mark this event in an appropriate way, by introducing into this House a proposal to give a pension to the veterans of 1866, among whom no regiment has a better list than the Tenth Royals of Toronto. If the minister wishes to commemorate this event and encourage the volunteers of this country, he could not bring forward a more popular proposal. There came under my notice the other day the case of one of these veterans who died in the poor house. The time has come when we should recognize in a substantial way the services of these men on behalf of their country.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: I would like to say that recognition has been given to these men, and it is one of the things that I am most proud of in connection with my record as Minister of Militia, that I was able to induce the British government to give to those who took part in resisting the attempted raid at that time recognition m the form of a suitable medal. For some 30 years, from 1866 to 1896, the services of those men had been utterly neglected and disregarded. When the present government came in and_ took the matter up, within a year of the time it took office, a medal was granted by Queen Victoria in recognition of their services. I wish to say too, that at that time the veterans from one end of the country to the other expressed themselves as entirely satisfied with what had been done.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair, I would like to draw the attention of the House to an article which appeared in the Toronto ' Globe ' of the. 21st instant; though I am not complaining of this particular article, which is simply a sample of articles which have appeared in the Liberal press throughout the length and breadth of Canada since this House reassembled. There appears to be an organized campaign for the purpose of misrepresenting the attitude of the opposition. I have no doubt that before the House reassembled the government had determined to go to the country, because it found itself between the devil and the deep blue sea. The devil was the ever-increasing sentiment in Ontario, and the eastern

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext:
provinces against reciprocity, and the deep blue sea was the fear that if they waited and bore the brunt of that sentiment they would have to bear the odium of refusing the west the additional representation to which they are justly entitled. But the government made their choice before we reassembled, of which I propose to give evidence later on; and so, having decided to deprive the west of the representation it is entitled to, they are trying to make the country believe that the opposition, by a reasonable discussion-as they say, by their obstruction-are preventing the government from giving the west that representation to which it is justly entitled; and they have come to this conclusion also because of the manly, straightforward and unanswerable argument presented by our leader, Mr. Borden, during his recent triumphal tour of the west, and the growing feeling against reciprocity there.
So I think I am safe in saying that it is part of the party tactics that the House should reassemble and when the opposition should express their views upon reciprocity the government should shout obstruction. I may say here that either the right hon. the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance (I am not sure which) has already stated in this House that every member on this side would be given an opportunity to express his opinions upon this measure, and that while they were so doing they would not be considered guilty of obstruction. Now, there are 55 members on this side of the House who have not had an opportunity of expressing themselves on the question of reciprocity, and none of the members who have spoken, have spoken twice. Notwithstanding that fact we are met with the statement in the Liberal press throughout the country that the opposition are obstructing. Now, what is the evidence before us, that the government had decided to go to the country before we reassembled. In the first place it is known that the government Printing Bureau is at work in the preparation of the voters' lists for the coming election. In the second place, while the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) made up his mind not to run again, since the adjournment of the House, he suddenly reconsidered his decision, and decided to become a candidate in North York, upon the assumption that the elections were to be held this fall. In the next place the Dominion Election Act provides that with respect to the unorganized districts in the province of Ontario, every year there shall be prepared a list of the voters in the constituencies, unless a proclamation is issued by the government stating thaj^ such list need not be prepared. I find that in the years 1909 and 1910, that such proclamation -was issued, but on the 17th of July

of the present year a proclamation was issued by the deputy of the Minister of Justice stating that the lists should be prepared in these unorganized districts, and that they should be accelerated, all this notwithstanding the fact the hon. Minister of Justice stated in the House the other day (21st July) that neither he nor any one else expected an election for one or two sessions yet. In addition to that, I have in my hand a document entitled ' Instructions for the guidance of1 returning officers,' printed in 1911, since we adjourned in May 19 last. I have seen cartloads of these documents around the building here, and I am advised that they are only printed in such large quantities in a year when an election is expected.
I think if these several facts are taken together, or even if the last fact is considered alone it is sufficient to prove that the government had made up their mind that they were going to the country before we re-assembled here, and that we are brought back for the purpose of assisting them in their party tactics of deceiving the west into the belief that the onus for non-redistribution is on us. I would point out to the right hon. the Prime Minister that on the 8th of March the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden), made a proposition to the government which the government did not accept, but which if it had accepted would have enabled the west to' have their'representation. Upon that occasion, Mr. Borden used these w'ords:
Now, Sir, I regard these proposals as reversing the policy of the people of Canada for the past thirty years, given by an unmistakable mandate at every election which has taken place during that period. What should be the course of the government at this time? Take the census, give the west its increased representation, then submit this question to the people of Canada and let them decide.
The government turned the proposition down four months ago, when they might have accepted it, have taken their census and have given the west their redistribution, It is not too late to do it yet, according to my way of thinking. The government can even now, accelerate their census, bring down their Redistribution Bill, and let reciprocity wait for a few months, until the west have been given their additional representation. We have existed 46 long years without reciprocity, and I think we can wait a few months longer. The hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) told us this session that never in the history of this country was Canada as prosperous as she is to-day. He told us that the trade of Canada to-day is $765,000,000-a high water mark in its history, and our surplus this year $30,000,000 the highest on record. Surely it is manifest that we can wait two or three
months longer without reciprocity, and in the meantime let the government bring down the Redistribution Bill, giving the west the representation to which they are entitled, and then go to the country. If that is not done, there is no other conclusion to be arrived at, but that we are here assisting the government in carrying out their farce, which will have the effect of depriving the west of their additional representation. We bn this side would be only too happy to face the electors on this great question, but we can only regret the course of the government will have the effect of depriving that great and growing country of their just rights in the matter of representation.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend rose for the purpose of trying to convince this House, and the country at large that His Majesty's opposition in this House is not obstructing the business of the government, and is not obstructing the reciprocity agreement, which has been before the House now since the 26th of January last. However, my hon. friend had not proceeded very far before he gave away his whole case. He protests that the opposition is not obstructing yet at the same time, he says:
' Let reciprocity wait.' If he is not obstructing, why should not reciprocity go on? That is what we on this side^ of the House want. We do not want reciprocity to wait. The hon. gentlemen, on the other side of the House told us what we already knew, and I thank my hon. friend for being so candid in the statement that they did not want reciprocity to go through, but wanted it to wait, and that they are trying in this House to prevent it from going on. We have had speeches of one kind and another-we have heard the same arguments repeated ad nauseam.
The other day one of the most respected members in this House prefaced his remarks by saying that there was nothing new to be said upon this question. That is perfectly true. Yet, he took three hours or more to say what had been said over and over again.
My hon. friends ask us: * Why should we not have a redistribution?' Well, the question of redistribution, is not before the House to-day, neither is the census, but the reciprocity agreement is before the House, and we can go on with it. If the hon. gentlemen wish to prevent an election let us go on with the reciprocity agreement, and there will be no election. I have nothing to hide in this matter, but will speak to the House with perfect candor. When I saw evidences of obstruction taking place in this House day after day [DOT]

speechtext:
Then, Sir, there are judges over us to judge between the government and the opposition. Surely these hon. gentlemen do not object to an election. They say they want an election, and when I tell them that they do not object, they cheer; but when we take steps to have an election, they find fault. But we understand all this. The last thing they want is to go before the country. Well, there is one way in which it is possible not to go to the country, and that is to pass the agreement, that the farmers of Canada may have the markets of the United States opened to their products. That is our position. My hon. friend tells me that they want redistribution. Well, redistribution Bills have been passed before now, and the usual regular course has been to take the census one year, and have redistribution the following year. The census was taken in 1881, 1891, and in 1901, and upon every occasion the Redistribution Bill was passed the following year-that is in 1882, in 1892, and 1902 respectively. If we follow the usual course, we have plenty of time for redistribution. It is true, my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) told us on the 8th of March that we should have passed the redistribution first. But he did not reflect at that time that the census could not be taken before the 1st of June. The law on that point was
changed some years ago. At the time of confederation, the first of April was fixed as the date for the taking of the census. But everybody knows that the first of April is not a good season for taking the census. The roads in many parts are not then favourable for travel, but the first of June, as we all know, is a most propitious season for the census work. The date was changed and nobody objected. Does my hon. friend believe 'that it is possible to have redistribution in Canada within three months of the taking of the census? It is impossible to have it done. It never has been done either under a Conservative government or under a Liberal government. The country is too large and the means of communication too imperfect. You must wait until the last return is in before you begin your redistribution. We will have redistribution next year. If the opposition chooses to go on with tactics of obstruction, as they have been doing, then we shall have to consider what is to be done. And if, in the last resort, the only way is to appeal to the people and ask them to pass judgment between us and the opposition, we are quite prepared and ready for it.

speechtext:
The Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has alluded to certain instructions which he said were communicated by him to the Secretary of State while he was in London. I have a very strong suspicion that those instructions were given to the Secretary of State before the Prime Minister went to London. Of course, they may have been repeated from there. So far as the frankness of my hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Middiebro) is concerned, to which the Prime Minister has alluded, I want to call his attention to the fact that on the 8th of March, the very date referred to, I moved in this House that, in view of considerations set forth in the resolution, this reciprocity agreement.
-should not be proceeded with until the electors shall have an opportunity of pronouncing upon its merits.
The Prime Minister knew what my view with regard to the matter was at that time. He is pressing for a vote in the House. Well, we are pressing for a vote in the country, a vote of the people. The right hon. gentleman, who professes himself to be a Liberal of the British school and ' a democrat to the hilt,' is unwilling to afford to the people the opportunity to give that vote except at the sacrifice of redistribution. I gave my advice on that point on the 8th of March last. It has been already quoted, but I think it was very good advice and it will do no harm to repeat it. I said:
W bat should be the course of the government at this time? Take the census, give the

west its increased representation, then submit this question to the people of Canada and let them decide. We held out to the United States for twenty years a standing offer of reciprocity, and they did not accept it. It will not lessen their respect for us if we permit them for a few years to put a standing offer of reciprocity upon their statute-book. We have worn some shoe leather in going to Washington ; as I said before, let the Americans wear out some shoe leather in coming to Ottawa. They are submitting these proposals to a new Congress; let us in Canada' submit these proposals to a new parliament.
I stand by those words. As a matter of fact, the Prime Minister magnified altogether the difficulty of enumerating the people. I am informed that in Great Britain, within two or three days the enumeration of the people is made known, and I believe that if, immediately after the 8th of March, when I asked them to follow this course, the government had taken steps to hasten the enumeration, that enumeration could have been completed before the end of June. We might then have had a Redistribution Bill before this parliament at the present moment.
For, after all, what is the position of the government in this matter? Their position is that, although the people of Canada have got on without reciprocity for forty-five years and have prospered remarkably well during that time in their great work of nation building, they cannot wait for six months in order to give a redistribution of representation and allow the people as a whole to pronounce upon this issue of reciprocity. I say that is an unreasonable proposition. I say, the course I suggested on the 8th of March would be the reasonable one. The position at that time was that the old Congress had just come to an end-it expired on the 4th of March-without having ratified this treaty. Surely, under these circumstances, it would not have been an unreasonable thing for the government of Canada to say that, as Congress had dissolved through effluxion of time without ratifying the treaty and the treaty must be ratified, if at all, by a new Congress, it might very well be ratified in Canada, if at all, by a new parliament, and after an appeal to the people.
Now, the Prime Minister is very pronounced in his strictures upon the opposition, for the course they have taken. I would like to repeat what my hon. friend from North Crey has said. It was announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) himself when he introduced this proposition, if I remember his words correctly, that every member of this House should have the right to express his convictions with regard to the matter and to give his reasons to parliament and to his constituents why he either approved or disapproved of this treaty.

I was endeavouring to get him to look at this from the standpoint of a minority who are desirous, in the first place, that there should be a redistribution in order that all parts of the country may have their proper representation, and who, in the next place, are anxious that the people of Canada should have an opportunity to pronounce upon this agreement before the policy of this country for the past forty years is absolutely reversed; and surely that should not be done without any mandate from the people. The right hon. gentleman is apparently inclined to follow a portion of the advice which I gave him on the 8th' of March last. I said this:
Take the census, give the west its increased representation, then submit this question to the people of Canada and let them decide.
He is willing to submit this question to the people of Canada and let them decide, but he is not willing to give the west the increased representation to which they are entitled. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I am bound to tell my hon. friend that the First Minister was thanking Heaven for something which hon. gentlemen at that time did not thank Heaven for, but for which they are thanking Heaven to-day. The Prime Minister was thanking Heaven for the better condition of life in Canada which had been brought about under the policy of a Liberal administration, and at that time hon. gentlemen opposite were preaching the cry that the policy of the Prime Minister and his colleagues was ruining the business of the country. Now, the hon. gentlemen have come to the point when they, too, thank Heaven for the commercial and financial prosperity which has come to the Dominion of Canada, and which they say is so good that they want it let alone.
Is this reciprocity? Yes it is substantially the same kind of reciprocity that was proposed in 1891 when Sir John Thompson issued his card to the electors of Antigon-ish, and asked to be returned because he and his colleagues were going to Washington to endeavour to bring about a reciprocity treaty, and he believed they would succeed. It was the same kind of reciprocity that the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) sought when he went to Washington. It is the same kind of reciprocity that was offered bv Sir Charles Tupper in 1887 and 1888. It is the same kind of reciprocity that every public man of eminence from the first day of July, 1867, to the 26th day of January, 1911, stood for before the public with the declaration that he was willing to have reciprocity, and would be glad to have it, always provided he could get it on fair and reasonable terms. If we had come before the country with a reciprocity treaty in the ordinary sense of the word, even then we might justly have asked the support of this parliament. But we realized that after all these years while it was still important to us, we thought, that we should	open up
the American market, we thought it better that we should not enter into a binding engagement for any particular term. And what do we find now? Hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House who, at one stage, said: Let us not make any binding treaty, let us have no entangling alliance-some of them and their friends in the press now turn around and say: ' What is the good of this reciprocity; you have no guarantee of its continuance?'

But take it all and all we thought it better we should not bind the parliament and the government of Canada for a given period of years, and we therefore arranged with the American negotiators that each party would make concessions in its tariffs. We said; We believe that these concessions will com-

mend themselves to the peiople of the United States and to the people of Canada; we believe that the arrangement when! confirmed by the respective legislative bodies will continue, not because anybody is bound to it but because the arrangement will prove so beneficial to the people of both countries that they will desire to continue it. maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.

And I am frank enough to say that we are looking at it from the point of view of Canada, and how it will benefit the people of this Dominion.
1 'am mo more called upon to sutain or defend what any one has said in the United States than o member of Congress would be called upcr to explain or defend what is said by any member of this House. I, therefore, think there is nothing in the interruption of my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes). I say that this measure is the very kind of reciprocity we have all been seeking for years, and even were it proposed "as a definite treaty, we might in the light of history reasonably ask the support of this parliament for the measure. But, in its present form, we can point the country to how much stronger is the situation. It is distinctly set out in the correspondence which forms the agreement that while we hope that this arrangement will commend itself to the judgment of the people of both nations, nevertheless we do not undertake to interfere with the liberty of Congress or of the Canadian parliament to make at any time any change in the arrangement which they see fit. That being the position, would it not seem logical and reasonable that hon. gentlemen who may not view the matter with much favour, should, under these circumstances, say: We will let this measure go through, if it is a good measure we will all be delighted by and by, and no harm will be done, but if it proves to be a bad measure the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier will be condemned for presenting it, and then the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier will pass away, and hon. gentlemen opposite will come to power, and they can repeal the measure. I believe, Sir, that that view will be taken by fair-minded men in the country. There are men-we know it with regret-who honestly oppose reciprocity, and we are sorry for it, and we respect their views as we wish them to respect ours, but these very men will surely say: What harm can be done for putting this in operation; if it is good as the Liberals say the country will benefit by it; if it is as bad as the Conservatives say, it is another nail in the coffin of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and his colleagues, and in a very short time in the natural order of events an election will come on, and a change of administration will follow, and the new government can repeal the measure if they choose. I have heard that view expressed by Conservatives in personal conversation with myself, and it is a reasonable view. The people of the country generally will I am sure say since this agreement does not profess to bind the people of Canada, since it leaves the parlia-

ment of Canada absolutely free to make such change in the fiscal policy of the country as parliament may please, it should have a chance. If it be the will of the people constitutionally expressed, to say this is a bad measure, then the in-coming government can re-impose the taxes we now propose to take off. In view of that circumstance, surely there is no fair and reasonable ground for a policy of obstruction in regard to the measure. I therefore, hold that the position taken by hon. gentlemen opposite from the beginning has not been fair and reasonable. Oh, but, they say, we want redistribution, and the west particularly wants it. Some hon. gentlemen opposite shed tears for the west because they are going to have an election without redistribution. Well, redistribution affects the whole country, but I suppose as a matter of fact it chiefly affects the west, and while the west wants redistribution there is one thing it wants more than redistribution, and that is reciprocity.

He cannot very easily be humbugged; he cannot be humbugged by a Conservative member who shouts for free agricultural implements, while his leader votes against free agricultural implements. The western farmer is a pretty keen fellow; he is intelligent perhaps above the average, and he wants redistribution although I do not think he is bothered very much about it. He wants reciprocity any way, and he knows there is a great difference between the situation in respect to redistribution, and the situation with respect to reciprocity. You can have redistribution by the will of this parliament at any moment, but you cannot have reciprocity at any moment by the sole will of the parliament of Canada. For many years while the Canadian parliament was ready to have reciprocity the people across the line were not ready for it. Sometimes there was a movement favourable to reciprocity, but what did we find? Any change in the fiscal policy of the United States requires a combination of the House of Representatives, which is now Democratic, the Senate, which is now Republican, and the president, who is now a Republican. A combination of these three is necessary to effect a change in the fiscal policy of the United States. Every effort for years to secure that combination has proved a failure down to the time of the present reciprocity agreement.
Mr. FIELDING

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: Wherein does it differ from any other law?

matter before the House and push it to a conclusion. That is what we are doing. Parliament is not bound. My hon. friend is not bound; I could not bind him if 1 would. No member of this parliament is bound. The government is bound, and whatever a government does in the name of the country binds in a certain sense the whole country, but as a matter of fact every member of this parliament remains unbound and absolutely free.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext:
I want to point out, first, that we do not bind the country; but I want to go and say that if we did bind the country, what right would these hon. gentlemen have to complain? They talk of two gentlemen going down to Washington, sitting in secret and binding the country. One hon. member made merry about this secret meeting at which the telephone was shut off and no one was allowed to come in. Has the hon. gentleman any idea that treaties or commercial arrangements of any sort are negotiated on the public streets? If two farmers want to make a deal about a mowing machine, they will probably sit down together in the kitchen of one of them and make an agreement. Do we not know that every business transaction between individuals in private life is negotiated privately? How was the treaty negotiated in bygone years under Conservative auspices? Was it negotiated on public streets? When Sir Charles Tupper went to Washington with Mr. Chamberlain in 1888 and 1889, and negotiated a treaty, which unfortunately the United States Senate never ratified, did he go on the public highway and invite the newspapers to come and listen to the negotiations? What childishness to put before the people of Canada. Every arrangement of this character, every important private negotiation, still more every important public negotiation, still more every international negotiation, is necessarily negotiated privately and in secret. But, Sir, in the previous treaties Canada has been in a measure
bound-bound for a definite period of years. We have not bound Canada to any definite period of years; but if we had done so, hon. gentlemen opposite would have no reason to complain. But there is this important difference: the Americans have reached a certain stage in this reciprocity matter which is of vital importance to us. Hon. gentlemen opposite at one time advanced the view-it was perhaps the most rational point in their argument-that we were not certain how the American Congress would deal with this matter. We knew that in times past, after certain progress had been made in the negotiations, the American Senate failed to approve. Why don't you wait, it was said, until the Americans decide for themselves? Well, we were not so much impressed with that argument as some of our hon, friends opposite were; but if there was anything in that argument, it is swept away to-day. Every step has been taken by the government of the United States. Loyally has the president kept his faith witn the government of Canada. He has put his great personality and his power behind that measure; he had quarrelled with members of his own party; he has called on patriotic Democrats and has said to them, ' I am sorry my own party is divided, come in and help this thing for the good of the country;' and he has won a response. Step by step he has done his part. The House of Representatives has passed the measure; the Senate of the United States has passed the measure; the president has recommended it, and the newspapers say that on Wednesday next, he will sign the Bill; and then, after having been for 40 years on the wrong side of the question, Uncle Sam will have put himself right. Are we to be right or wrong? We have been right in the past. We have always said to the Americans that we would deal with them on fair and reasonable grounds, but they would not consent. Row the current has changed. They have recognized the injustice-shall I say that?-at all events, the error of their way for the last 40 years in their trade relations with Canada. They have practically said, We think we have been wrong; we desire to come and make a Eair and reasonable arrangement. They have made a fair and reasonable arrangement. The only surprising thing in the minds of many Canadians is that we succeeded in making so good an arrangement.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext:
It is a good arrangement for the great west, and the great west is anxious for it this very year, with the prospect of a crop of 200,000,000 bushels of wheat. The west wants to know which is the best market. Shall we sell it to England? Very well, if England wants it; but if there is a better market across the bor-



der, who will say the western farmer shall not have the right to send his wheat across the border?
A few years ago the government of Newfoundland entered into an arrangement with the government of the United States under which the fish of Newfoundland was to be admitted into the United States free of duty while the fish of Canada would not be so admitted. The Canadian government made a strong protest and for some years they succeeded in preventing the government' of Newfoundland from making that agreement. Why? Because they said ' Canada wants free fish, and because we want to arrange matters so that Canada, as well as Newfoundland, shall get the benefit of the arrangement.
To-day we offer the fishermen of Canada that which the Conservatives, wanted for them in that quarrel, and we know that the best farmers, the best representatives of the farmers, throughout the country all approve of it. It is a good thing for the grain grower. It is -a good thing for the manufacturer, because we have achieved that which they said could not be done. We have achieved a reciprocity in natural products, without having to make any important concessions in the matter of manufactures.
This reciprocity is a good thing for the manufacturer, and I venture respectfully to repeat a word of advice which I offered them not long ago. I say unhesitatingly that from the point of view of the manufacturers of Canada this reciprocity agreement is a good arrangement, are. h ' socr through, we may reasonably say to the western farmer: ' Well, you cannot have all you want in this wicked world, but this goes a long way towards meeting your demands, and we can fairly ask you to give and take, and let the eastern manufacturer have a fair show,' and we believe they will do it. But, if perchance the manufacturers in their great power should unite in opposing, and possibly condemning, or even defeating this measure, then there will rise up in that western country a storm cloud bigger than a man's hand, and the end will be a change in the fiscal policy of the country, which the manufacturers will find much greater than anything they conceived of.
Mr. SCHAE'FNER. Neither the hon. gentleman nor his party would think of hurting the manufacturers. The right hon. the Prime Minister says he will not hurt the manufacturers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext:
We say we have not hurt the manufacturers. We know, nevertheless, that many of the manufacturers have been needlessly alarmed, and we know that to-day they are opposing us in this matter. However, I am free to say Mr. FIELDING
that I think they have made a mistake, because it will be in their interests as well as in the interests of the country to have the agreement go through.
Redistribution and reciprocity-the west wants both-but they do not want them both at the same moment, and they do not expect them both at the same moment. In the year 1891, the census was taken on the 1st day of April, yet on the very eve of that census-in the month of March, I think, Sir John A. Macdonald appealed to the people, and we had a general election. The census came along a few weeks afterwards. The west had to wait for its redistribution for three or four years, and it had nothing in particular to wait for. Today I do not know whether the west will have to wait for redistribution or not, but if it has to wait, it will be because there is a more important measure than redistribution before it. As I stated, reciprocity in days gone by has been desired by all, but never before has it been within our grasp. At the present time it is offered to us, and the question is, ' Shall we take it?' We, on behalf of the Liberals of Canada, say, we believe the people want it and will take it. We challenge you to let it pass in this House, and a year hence we will meet my hon. friends in any manner they, wish. If they believe this is a dangerous measure, it can only be dangerous for a few short months. The elections will come on, in the ordinary course of events, before many months have passed. Redistribution will come on, and then they will have an opportunity not only of sweeping out this government-which they desire so much-but they will have an opportunity of repealing this measure and putting on the taxes which we wish to take off.
After nearly half a century we have now found the psychological moment when reciprocity is within our grasp. Shall we take it? ' Yes,' will be the voice of the people.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is not reciprocity. It is revolution.

speechtext: We do not object. Let the hon. gentleman go on.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext:
This is not. reciprocity. It is revolution. It is commercial union, or at least partial commercial union which must end in complete commercial union. The hon. gentleman who has just preceded me (Mr. Fielding) says that the agreement meets with the

approval of the Republican party, the Democratic party, the Senate and President of the United States, This may be perfectly true. But why is it so? Because, for the first time, Canada has admitted the President of the United States into her councils in making the tariff of this country, It is the most humiliating thing that has ever occurred in this country. It is the first time a president of the United States by using the big stick-as he used it on the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) in Albany, in connection with the Payne-Aldrich treaty-forced him to make a change in the tariff law of this country. ' Then,' he said, ' you must come back to Washington and make an arrangement in regard to the duty,' and the hon. Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) went to Washington and allowed the President of the United States, in secret negotiation, to participate in the making of the tariff of this country.
_ Where did we get our independence in regard to the tariff? We achieved it from the mother country, in days gone by. It was a hard thing to achieve, and once we had it we used it in bringing about a national policy, and making this country great. Now that national policy has been a success and our commercial and tariff independence has been vindicated, yet, we propose to give it over to the United States. No wonder all the parties of the United States are united in desiring to have this thing passed, because by so doing we are admitting them into participation in the making of the tariff of Canada. Surely that is not what we achieved our commercial independence for. We are putting the mother country out, to let the American people in.	.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: No, we are not, and you know better.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: Yes, we are, and I will give you my proof. I want to show how radical this change is, and how it departs from all the traditions of the past. In years gone by we have had tariff proposals submitted to this House, and argued from all points of view, and interest; but inasmuch as this tariff has the approval of the United States, and cannot be changed without their consent and without negotiations, a revolution has been proposed in the country. And the proof of it is that the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton), the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German), and the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Harris) has to leave their party because they could not go to the government to have the tariff changed but had to go to the President of the United States.

That is rot.

That is all very well for the hon. member from Nova Scotia (Mr. Black) he does not like it. But the reason he does not like it is that, it is true. The Prime Minister, when in England recently, was not the friend of the Empire; and to-day, before the Empire and the world, he appears as the friend and colleague of the President of the United States. He has allowed the President of the United States to have a say in making the tariff of Canada. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has said we can rescind this tariff when we like. The President called a special session of Congress in order to deal with this matter, and they have passed this agreement. If Canada passes the agreement under those conditions, it is to be said that we can so disregard the President and Congress as to repeal that agreement within a year? The United States would have every reason for a hostile attitude towards Canada if we went into an agreement of this kind sanctified, as we. may say, by legislation and then repealed it within a short time. We could not repeal it without entering into negotiations with the President of the United States, if we want to keep our good faith.
I have just said that this is a great organic change in regard to our tariff the like of which was never proposed in this House before. Hitherto, we have made the tariff of this country in this House. This time, it has been made out of the House, and that is a change that every Canadian should view with alarm. Heretofore, Parliament has been able to modify any tariff propositions brought down. I remember when Sir John Thompson and Mr. Foster proposed tariff changes, it was, as they said to lop away the mouldering branches. But their proposals did not meet with the views of the majority of this House, and the result was that the Government of the day had to modify their proposals. In this case there can be no modi fication and, this is to be said of a tariff which, as has already been pointed out, was made by two men who did not know all the trade conditions of this country. I could name a county in New Brunswick that will be injured by this agreement.

mons to make changes, I say that power has been seized by the cabinet-by a section of the cabinet for not all were consulted-and that junta in the cabinet undertake to make the tariff of Canada in collusion with the President of the United States, and that tariff cannot be changed unless.

speechtext: What is the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Turriff) opinion. I come back to mine that for the first time in the history of Canada our tariff has been made outside this House. And the proof is the rush the Americans make to grab it when the offer is made, and we are letting the President of the United States have a hand in making our tariff.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) allow me a question? I wish to understand his argument. Does he mean to say that we have made the tariff with the United States as evidenced by the Bill passed by the Senate of that country on Saturday last?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext:
There was no change made there. The gag was put on, and the same unconstitutional course pursued as is pursued here. And, for political reasons, they joined in it in order to have a say in this country. This is not only an organic change in our constitution, but it is the introduction of commercial union. In fact, it is partial commercial union. The right hon. the Prime Minister is still a commercial unionist, and it is the old commercial unionist who was discredited by the people in 1891 who will be discredited this year if he goes to the country. And when the right hon. gentleman said that he and his party were the champions of redistribution, and, though his organs demand it, yet, .the responsibility for the failure to pass redistribution, should it not be passed, must be upon him and his friends. I wish to give a proof that commercial union is back of this. Commercial union was the thing that united Germany. These were scattered and divided states, but commercial union drew them together so that they became one country. And the design of the United States is to absorb Canada by a partial and then a complete system of commercial union, if .they can get Mr. MACLEAN.
the people of Canada to go into it. Once the ball is started rolling, this will be the effect, unless the people of Canada unite. That is the real question in all this. Hon. gentlemen opposite have presented it to the people as a question of markets, of profits, of dollars, I hope that this question will be considered in its effect upon our national institutions. If the Americans can succeed in controlling our tariff, they will wipe out our British institutions. As President Taft said:	This will wipe out
trade between the mother country and other states of the empire. What are dollat-3 compared with our institutions? We have British institutions which give the people of Canada better government than the people of the United States enjoy. Reciprocity is supported in the United States because the leaders, and the trusts there wish to divert the attention of the people from the problems with which they are faced. And another thing is to make their country greater and give it the right to intervene in the affairs of Canada. I say this is the most deplorable piece of legislation ever proposed in this country. And I believe that when the people come to vote on this agreement they will vote against it, because it means the sacrifice of our institutions. And, as I have said before in this House, I know of nothing so dangerous to the ideals of the people of Quebec-' Our laws, our language, our institutions '-as to give the United States a say -in the affairs of Canada. They will drive British institutions out of this country if they can be driven out. But my contention is that no effort in this direction on the part of the United States or of hon. gentlemen opposite can be successful. The heart of Canada is sound, and it is British. It is for imperial trade all around the world, and we are going to have that band of English speaking people all around the world trading one with the other, in spite of Mr. Taft, in spite of the right hon. gentleman and his government. Our destiny is not with the United States, it is away from the United States. Hon. gentlemen are trying to drive us that way, as they tried to drive this country twenty odd years ago; and Sir John A. Macdonald said then, as every Canadian says now, ' A British subject I was born, and a British subject I will die. We will keep British institutions in Canada.

1C026

My Lord,-I have the honour to send to your Lordship to-day a telegraphic message ill cipher, of which the following is the substance :
With reference to my telegram of the 10th inst., this government is desirous of proposing a joint commission such as that of 1871, with authority to deal without limitation

Mark the word:
-without limitation, and to prepare a treaty respecting the following subjects:
1. Renewal of the reciprocity treaty of 1851, with the modifications required by the altered circumstances of both countries and with the extensions deemed by the commisison to be in the interests of Canada and of the United States.
And is my hon. friend also aware that the definition which Sir Charles Tupper gave in parliament to these words 'without limitation'; was that the Canadian government were making an unrestricted offer of reciprocity to the United States?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman can read the dispatch, and he and the man who wrote the dispatch are responsible for it. I am responsible here for my position in this House, and to the trust that has been reposed in me by the people of South York, and they are against this proposition, they are against the raid that is made on the nationality of Canada, and they intend to vote against it. Now this proposal, as I have said, is revolutionary, and it is to be followed by the threat that the Minister of Finance made here today, and the farmers of this country will be justified, if they have no protection, in coming here next year and asking for the removal of what was once described in one of my election contests as the last vestige of the National Policy from the statute-book of Canada. That is what is ahead of the people of Canada today. We are to have no more protection of our industries, we are to allow the president and Congress of the United States to have a say in our tariff, and Canada is to become suzerain of the United. States, or we will become states of the union and send senators to Congress. We will have Canada reduced to the position of being a number of states in the American republic. Now we do not want that, and the issue is before us. The Minister of Finance today made it a mere issue of profit, or dollar, what the western farmer was going to get out of it. Now I venture to say that the western farmer has had his eyes opened; I venture the prediction that the people of the west will return a majority against this proposition. A great change
of opinion is going on throughout Canada over this pact.

speechtext:
The remarks of my hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) seem to have raised a storm of dissent from the government. The government find itself in an extraordinary and pitiable condition. I confess that I never heard a more pitiable exhibition in the shape of oratory than that which has fallen from the lips of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance on this occasion. Why, Sir, of all the childish positions I never heard the like before. Schoolboy tactics, childish tactics, the most pusillanimous kind of tactics, the most feeble kind of protest, to come from hon. gentlemen who are supposed to have a sense of the dignity and responsibility of the government of this great country. Sir, what did the Finance Minister say on the floor of this House in February last? what did the Minister of Customs say in February last, and what have they said on the hustings? What did the Finance Minister say in the city of Montreal? Ever since they introduced this pact they have been saying that it will not be many months very much earlier than you expect, before this whole thing will be submitted to the people of Canada. And did the opposition dissent from that? Not at all, the opposition never have dissented. The government have been crying that only for us they were willing to submit this matter to the people at once. They are working off their bluff upon the opposition and the people of Canada, when the very last thing that the government desires is an appeal to the people. How did the Minister of Finance vote upon

dulge in are very largely imported from, or through Great Britain, and if we thus indulge in luxuries our importations from Great Britain will largely increase, to the mutual advantage of the two countries, particularly of Great Britain. We have not on our side had any door open to her products; we have not given them any great advantage, but, with an extended trade, with the development of our resources, and the increase in our revenue which must necessarily follow, we could fairly well say: ' We can and will increase this preference from a 331 per cent to a 50 per cent preference in favour of Great Britain.
Many hon. gentlemen in dealing with this question ask what the electorate are going to do. I do not pretend to have any prophetic sense, but I do say this, and I will make it as a prophecy that when the people of Canada are called upon, whether it be sooner or later, to deal with the question of reciprocity, or of the expansion of the trade relations between these countries, they will deal with it from one standpoint alone. It will not be with them as it is too often here, as a case of merely playing, they will not be indulging in the game of politics; the people of Canada, and particularly the people of eastern Canada, for whom I can more readily speak, will deal with it from a business standpoint, from the standpoint of their bread and butter; and I think I can fairly say, speaking from that eastern standpoint, that it is to the advantage of their bread and butter that they shall have an additional market, that they shall have at least the choice of an additional market, and that they shall not be confined to one purchaser, or even to two, but that they shall have as many purchasers as it is possible to have. It is all very well to say that this constituency, or that section of the country will do this or do that. I believe the people will largely deal with the question in the way I have indicated, and if the electorate of Canada do that, certainly I will be content and I think every hon. member in this House should be content.
My hon. friend has said that because this member or that member lias not spoken there is some doubt as to his convictions. I would be very sorry to be judged from that standpoint. My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) did not speak, it is true, in this House on the question of reciprocity. I did not speak, but I would not wish my views to be judged from that fact. I do know that the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) dur-

ing the month of June spent practically all his time campaigning, not only in Pictou, but in every county of the province of Nova Scotia. Doing what? Advocating reciprocity.

speechtext:
I want to be accurate I would not wish to say every county, I would say almost every county. I think that can be very well taken in a Pickwickian sense, but there is this to be conceded that he was actively campaigning and he was advocating reciprocity. Whether he bearded the lion in his den in the county of Colchester I do not know but perhaps he thought discretion was the better part of valour in that case.
But the people of Canada are not concerned as to who made speeches and who did not, it does not matter much whether this man goes down and somebody else come up in his place. We should have at least the earnestness and the courage of our convictions and not hide ourselves behind our electorate or our constituency.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext:
The hon. member for West Algoma' says hear, hear. Then let us have a vote on this question. Then we will have at least a decision before the people of this country as to what the mind of the representatives of the people is as indicated by their votes and that must be the best indication. While challenges have *been thrown out, if I were in a position to throw challenges to anybody I would throw a challenge not merely to hon. members opposite but to those on this side as well, let us have a vote, let us each one record his views. There need then be no occasion for aspersions on the attitude of this or that member, there need be no reflections upon the course that this or that hon. member has taken. The hon. member for West Algoma (Mr. Boyce) had better refer to some very apt words once uttered by Abe Lincoln, if he will not consider me disloyal in making the quotation. Lincoln said: There is so much bad in the best of us and so much good in the worst of us that it hardly behooves any of us to talk about the rest of us. I think that is a very good motto to apply all around. However, it would not be a matter of reflection upon any hon. member in this House if he could stand in his place and give voice to his conviction by his vote as recorded on
the journals of this House. I think it would be well to have such a record and to have it at the earliest possible moment. There certainly would be no obstruction,
I am sure, as to that. Of course I would not for a moment insinuate that there is any desire to obstruct.	_
People can draw their own inferences, but I do think hon. gentlemen opposite are . very anxious to change places, and they have the hope; or at least they express the hope, that they have a good chance ot doing so. But, possibly, in striving to weave the purple robe of power, they have indulged in what some people may call, aye, what some people do call, obstruction. Are they going to pursue that course in the face of 'the attitude of the United States, when that great nation tenders us a contract signed and executed for the extension of our mutual trade. Under existing conditions, the responsibility resting upon us is, I believe, greater than has ever been placed before upon the legislators or the people of Canada. I venture to think that is the view the people will take of it. l believe they are wondering why a great political partv should fling itself m the face or the wheels of progress, to prevent the consummation of that which it is believed will stimulate the development of our trade and commerce.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: If the hon. member admires the United States so much, would lie please tell us why they took the great privilege of reciprocity from us m l*bt>.
