Well, we are not in the union yet, and i fervently pray we never will be.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext:
I think the hon. member's question should be barred by the Statute of Limitations. At all events it lies in the mouth of no party to raise it because, since 1866, Sir John Macdonald, Sir Charles Tupper, Sir John Thompson, the Hon. George E. Foster, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Alex. Mackenzie, Edward Blake, George Brown, and all the great statesmen of Canada, since the declaration made by the United States Senator at Detroit in 1866, have advocated reciprocity with the United States.
Mr MACDONELL (Toronto), Is the hon gentleman (Mr. Emmerson) not dealing wholesale in post-mortems just now?

10C44

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: I am merely trying to lay the ghosts that hon. gentlemen opposite are seeking to raise. To-day, my hon. friend from York (Mr. Maclean) raised the ghost of the disruption of the empire, and the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Boyce) raised the ghost of the termination of our national existence and presented a map of British North America carved into smithereens. I have, Mr. Speaker, strong views in favour of reciprocity, and I think it will be admitted that I have^ the courage to express my views. Had Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his government taken the responsibility of declining to negotiate with the United States when they made the request to us I wonder what would have been the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite. I know what my attitude would have been. I have been a Liberal all my life, but strong as I am in adherence to Liberal principles, if this government had taken upon itself the responsibility of declining to enter into these negotiations, much as I respect Sir Wilfrid Laurier I would consider that he should forfeit my support and confidence and I do not think that I would hesitate to tell him so. I have expressed views in this House contrary to the views of the government, but I am happy to know that in this instance^ the policy they have adopted meets with my whole-hearted approval and shall receive my most cordial support.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: The argument addressed to the House by the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) simmered down was in effect, an appeal to this side of . the House to let a vote be taken upon this question. In answering that, it might be well to remind hon. members that the position of the Conservative party on this measure has been clearly set forth from the very beginning of this debate, and had the government seen fit to adopt the position taken by the opposition with regard to it there would have been no question of obstruction and this debate would have ended long ago. On the 26th of January last, the Minister of Finance brought down his resolution to amend the tariff of 1907 and after listening to his full presentation of the case and taking time to consider it m all its bearings, the leader of the opposition moved an amendment on the 8th of March which set forth clearly and fully the position which we have maintained up to the present time and which answers the question of the hon. member (Mr. Emmerson): why not take a vote upon it? Let me remind him of the exact position by reading that resolution, and I think he will be surprised, after his remarks of the last few minutes, to find that he is placed on record _ as having voted against the very position he now asks the House to take.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext:
That all the words after the word that' in the proposed motion be omitted and the following substituted therefor:
The reciprocal agreement embodied in the resolutions submitted to this House by the Minister of Finance on the 26th day of January last, was also submitted on the same day by special message of the President to the Congress of the United States of America which was then in session.
That the said session has now expired and Congress has failed to approve and carry out the said agreement.
That a considerable length of time must necessarily elapse before the said agreement can be dealt with by Congress at a special session.
The next clause answers one other point made by the hon. member for Westmorland, when he referred to the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean), who said that this involved great constitutional changes. This paragraph covers his entire argument and fully vindicates the position taken by the hon. member for South York:
That the fiscal changes by the said agreement are of a far reaching character and constitute a substantial reversal of the policy which has been approved by the people of Canada.
The final summing up was as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the said resolutions should not be proceeded with until the electors shall have had an opportunity of pronouncing upon their merits.
All that we asked, and all that we have continued to ask, is that the electors shall have an opportunity of pronouncing upon these merits; and yet at this late hour, after nearly six months of wasted time, we find the hon. member for Westmorland, in his place in the House, saying, why not vote upon it? actually accusing men on this side of the House of being afraid of their principles, of trying to hedge themselves about and taking two positions in regard to this question.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: I made no insinuation.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: The basis of his argument, if there was any argument, was that we were afraid to go to the people. He said he himself advocated going to the people. There is the resolution clearly and distinctly asking only one thing.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: Will my hon. friend pardon me? I think he must have misunderstood me. What I was advocating was that we have a straight vote on this question in this House. I was not talking about a vote in the country. Before we have that, let us have a straight vote here.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext:
Exactly, and it was a straight vote we had in this House on this amendment. We placed our position fair-

ly and squarely before the country, that this agreement was so far reaching in its consequences that we should submit it to the people of Canada and ask their verdict upon it; and if there has been waste of time and obstruction, that is due to the government and the government alone.
I would like to say a word or two with regard to the very remarkable admission made by the right hon. leader of this government, an admission that I know was wrung from him much against his will by the strong argument advanced by the hon. member for West Algoma (Mr. Boyce), when he had placed before him his own words in which he had declared over and over again that we were through with reciprocity, that never again would this question be brought up; and I wish to point out to my hon. friend from Westmorland that these utterances were made since the date to which he has referred. I have the official documents to show that in 1899, in 1901, in 1907 and in 1909, at the Imperial Conferences in those yearns, the right hon. the Prime Minister said that Canada was through with reciprocity; and in the elections of 1904 and 1908 that question was not an issue. It seems difficult to impress upon hon. gentlemen opposite what these quotations from the speeches of the right hon. leader of the government mean. Indeed, I may say that as a young member of this House, during the three sessions that I have sat here listening to the various debates, I have been amazed at some of the things that I have learned with regard to the policy of the right hon. leader of the government. Over and over again 1 have witnessed the spectacle of various Hansards bcdng brought in from the library and quotations read from them of absolutely contrary opinions advanced by the hon. leader of the government on every great public question before this country; and gradually the conviction has been forced upon me that he has no fixed principle, and that he is ever ready, by pleasant phrases, eloquent in themselves, to obtain the plaudits of the people regardless of what the practical results may be. One is forced to that conclusion, however much against his will. At the Imperial Conference, of 1907 the right hon. leader of the government said:
But so far as legislation can influence trade we have done everything possible to push our trade towards the British people as against the American people.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: May I say I did not in the least dispute that. My objection was not, as I think I made clear, in any sense to complain of the Canadian preference; on the contrary, I recognize both its intention and its effect. Mv point was that natural conditions were such that it was inevitable that the Americans should get the best of it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext:
Not only have we done it by preference, by legislation, but we have forced our trade against the laws of nature and geography. If we were to follow the laws of nature and geography between Canady and the United States, the whole trade would flow from south to north, and from north to south. We have done everything possible by building canals and subsidizing railways to bring the trade from west to east and east to west so as to bring trade into British channels. All this we have done recognizing the principle of the great advantage of forcing trade within the British Empire.
There is the whole kernel-if there is any kernel-of the remarks made by the right hon. the leader of the government. It is contained in this one phrase 'AH this we have done recognizing the advantage of forcing trade within the British Empire.' It was not merely a matter of sentiment, it was not merely that they must give the mother country an advantage, but it was because he distinctly declared that he recognized it was an advantage for the people of Canada to force the trade within the Empire.
Then, why this sudden change of sentiment? If it was an advantage in 1907, why is it not an advantage in 1911? We had the quotation cited by the hon. member for West Algoma (Mr. Boyce)-'thank heaven that time has passed.' Let me read the exact words of the right hon. leader of the government:
Canada to-day is not in favour of reciprocity. There was a time when Canadians, beginning with myself would have given many things to obtain the American market, but, thank Heaven, these days are past and over.
Yet when pressed by the hon. member from West Algoma (Mr. Boyce) as to why they were now asking for a renewal of the treaty the right hon. the Prime Minister said because those days had returned again. It would be interesting to have a frank admission as to what was in the mind of the right hon. the leader of the government when he said he thanked heaven that these days were passed for ever. Surely no man would thank Providence that something had passed away unless he felt it was for his own advantage or for the advantage of the country. Still, we have t'he right hon. gentleman thanking heaven that these days had gone for ever. Then, we have the most astonishing statement on the floor of the House that these days were back upon us. I think we should very much like to know what are these days which are now confronting us and compelling us to seek aid from the nation to the south. In that connection it must be appropriate to read what was said by another very prominent Liberal A leader for many years, and premier of Hie great province of Ontario. This was not away

back yeans ago, as my bon. friend . from West Algorna said, but in the year' 1910. Here is what Sir Geo. Boss said before the Toronto Club:
Iti 1866, when the old treaty was repealed, we were poor in banking capital, in skilled labour, in agriculture and manufactures. A treaty then would have afforded some relief- to-day conditions are different-diff irent bicause the repeal of the treaty removed every prop on which we had formerly leaned and the true temper of our Anglo-Saxon spirit was roused to action. I think no country in the world affords a better illustration of public spirit than Canada when the United States in 186G flung our poverty in our faces and told us our only choice was starvation or annexation.
I wonder what was in the mind of the right hon. gentleman when he said that these days were upon us again, when it was necessary to call for the unlocking of the door which had 'been flung in our faces I do not intend to weary you with following up this line of argument, but would like to call it to the attention of the House IS orS'?r ^at the right hon. gentleman and th'e Liberal press may be able to explain to the .people of Canada during the coming campaign what was in the minds of the present government when they said that these days of darkness, of distress, and poverty are upon us again, .so that we are compelled to seek succour .from the great nation to the south of us.
'Another argument wais advanced this afternoon by the hon. the Finance Minister. It was a very specious argument and one that, I think, I am safe in saying, occupied at least three quarters of this entire address. This argument has already been taken on the .platform -by the Liberal speakers throughout the country and is one which is likely to play ,a very important part in the coming campaign. When I referred to this argument .as being specious I spoke advisedly. The hon. Finance Minister said 'It i.s true there are those of my own persuasion, Liberals, who honestly differ from me in regard to this question. However much I may regret that, I would say I think there is an argument Which seems to appeal to me and it ought to appeal to them and to every reasonable man-it is this there is nothing fixed about this treaty. We have been blamed for going down to Washington and binding th-e people of Canada. However, I say to you that there is nothing to prevent a change being made .at .any time in regard to this treaty ' Now, I say unhesitatingly, that while technically he was stating -the fact, yet in practical results he was speaking what would not .and .could not possibly work out. Indeed, the hon. the Finance Minister himself was so convinced of the weakness of his argument that a little later on he said he doubted whether it would not be
Mr. GOODEVE
better if the treaty had been for a fixed time. What are the facts in connection with this? Gan we alter or phange this treaty at any time? I would like to ask the hon. Finance Minister supposing we decided to allow this resolution to go through, and the agreement was duly signed and sealed, if within two months we wished to alter it would he, and would the people of the United States consider that we had honorably kept faith with them? Bear in mind the position he laid before this House in bringing down his pact, that we were not to change it by one iota. The agreement as made by himself and his colleagues was to be passed just as it stood. Over and over again he had stated to thi-s House that we are in honour bound to pass it just as it was brought down. If that was the case, I would like the hon. the Finance Minister, or the Minister of Customs-who is in his place-to tell me the exact date when he would consider us as being .absolutely free to alter or change this -agreement. Would it .be at the end of two months? Would it be at the end of six months? or would be feel that the people of Canada bad done all they were in honour bound to do if they tried it for one year and then .altered it because it was found to be unsatisfactory? I think not

at least I believe the United States would not .so consider it.
And so I could go on to say, one, or two, or three years. And we see that on that account it certainly would not be keeping, faith; so we are bound by this agreement as fully as if we had entered into a treaty, with the added disadvantage that it is not for any fixed time, and there is therefore, there is always the possibility, as the Minister of Finance has said of disturbing trade.
Now, another argument in the same line. On the 30th of March, 1910, a committee was appointed to meet with the representatives of the United States in regard to the placing of the surtax-because, forsooth, we had made an agreement with France affecting a certain number of articles, and for that reason the United States threatened us with this discrimination. And the Minister of Finance came on this floor and proposed giving them certain concessions and defended his course in so doing. He said we did not want a tariff war. Well, Sir, if, when we were not bound to them in any way, the hon. gentleman felt justified in saying to our people that we were compelled to make certain concessions to the United States in order to avoid a tariff war, how much more would that argument apply once this pact went into force.
There is a further argument on the same line. I have only been here three sessions. _ But again and again, as certain changes in our tariff have been asked for by some of our own people, I have heard

the Minister of Finance, even while admitting that the changes proposed might be of some benefit to those who asked for them, yet a stable tariff is better for the people of Canada than constant changing and tinkering, and for that reason he refused to make the changes. And the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) says ' Hear, hear.' I agree with him; the argument is in itself a good one. But apply it to this pact. If the minister's argument is to be accepted, what would be our condition in regard to stability of tariff? If we did not know it from week to week when our tariff would be changed, what would be the condition of our trade? Take, for instance, the fruit trade. What will be the result of the Niagara fruit men, and the British Columbia fruit men? The handlers of the product, the commission men would make their arrangements wth the fruit producers of the United States, and the industry would be changed from the present channel into the new one. That itself would mean loss. But, once these changes are made, any man or government would hesitate to alter these conditions knowing the injury that would result. Any man who has followed the political history of the nation to the south of us knows how the commerce of that country is disturbed every presidential year. And why? Because in every presidential campaign the tariff issue has been to the fore, and commerce is practically at a standstill awaiting the result, knowing that the change in fiscal conditions would mean much loss or gain to the people. Are we to place ourselves in that position? Are we to be tied to the tail of the fiscal tariff of the United States? It is easy for the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Customs to stand on this floor and say: We can try this, and if we do not like it we can change it. As I say, technically that is true, but practically and in fact, as I have shown, there are reasons why it is impracticable and impossible, and no man knows better than the two ministers who made the pact, and brought it down to this House. So, I say, it is no wonder that the Finance Minister pleaded with his own side, and with the press gallery-for I saw him watching the reporters when he made his argument-and even pleaded with men on this side, that we should make the trial on the ground that it could do no harm. But he knows that this is not a question to be played with; it is too great, too far-reaching, too vital to the great commercial interests of this Dominion to be played with >by any set of men. We are here to deal with these questions with a view to their broad national effect. For more than forty years we have gone on and prospered. Year after year in this House we have heard the minister say-and his 317
words have been repeated throughout the length and breadth of Canada by the Liberal press-that the progress of the country has been marvellous under the fiscal system adopted in 1878. My hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Emmersom) said that Sir John Thompson and Sir John Abbott and Sir John A. Macdonald had asked for reciprocity. But that was before they had adopted the great National Policy. But when that was put into effect, and as a result the poverty and distress-this hour of darkness so graphically referred to by Sir George Boss-passed away. We have developed our great natural resources while the people of the south have wasted and largely destroyed theirs. The time has come when we have reached the position in which we can manufacture our products against any people in the world; and at this time the people of the United States are very anxious to come in and partake of our great natural resources.
I do not propose at this time to go into that subject, though I should like to deal with the question .of lumber and pulp as affecting particularly my own province of British Columbia. But I confine myself simply to the remarks of the First Minister and the Finance Minister. I say again, I would like these hon. gentlemen to lay before the people how the Finance Minister proposes to try this pact, as he says, without disturbing the commercial interests of this great Dominion.
On that ground, if no other, I say that before a measure of such far reaching consequences is placed on the statute-book of Canada, we should weigh it well, and we should give the people of Canada an opportunity of expressing their will with regard to it. Every man knows in his heart that once this pact goes into effect we cannot change it at our will. It seems that we are turning back from the promised land into the bondage of the fiscal tariff of the United States, there is no question of that. Undoubtedly we should be tied up with them, we are bound more or less to consult them in whatever we do hereafter with regard to it.
I wish to refer to an extraordinary remark the Minister of Finance made this afternoon. It is true, he says, that we sent a message to the manufacturers saying that this agreement would not injure them, that it would only help the farmers and consumers. Here one naturally asks how, if it is going to aid farmers by giving them higher prices, it is also going to help the consumers by giving them lower prices. But there is another phase of this matter. The minister's statement was carefully worded. As the member for West Algoma said, the government undertook with one hand to hold a pistol to the hon. gentleman for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), and in the



other hand they held out this sonorifie. And so I may say the Minister of Finance this afternoon, undertook with one hand to hold out a badge of peace to the manufacturers of this country, and with the other hand he held out a threatening pistol. There is no doubt of the meaning underlying his words. In almost these words he says: We have given the people of the west, not all they asked, but all we are prepared to give them at this time; and I would like to warn the manufacturers that if they continue in their opposition to this agreement the time may come when they will find themselves in a worse position than they are at present; but if they are prepared to lie low and to cease their opposition, they may receive no further harm. In other words, the Minister of Finance asks the manufacturers to give up their rights of citizenship in order to purchase immunity from the attacks of this government. That was the attitude of the Minister of Finance towards the manufacturers. But his government does not reckon with the people of Canada. This government will find that the people of Canada will not tamely submit to be trampled upon, nor will they allow any government to take from them their constitutional rights and privileges.

speechtext: I have not spoken at all during the discussion of this question, therefore I may be permitted to make a few remarks in answer to some of the observations of my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Goodeve), and also to refer to the quotations which imy hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) has made as to the attitude of the leaders of the Conservative party in the past. I understand my hon. friend from Kootenay (Mr. Goodeve) to admit that it was true that the Conservative party was at one time in favour of reciprocity, but that was before the promulgation of the National Policy of 1879. Did I understand my hon. friend correctly?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext:
Then my hon. friend must have forgotten that upon the very last occasion when the Conservative party appealed successfully to the country they declared themselves unequivocally in favour of reciprocity with the United States. That was twelve years after the National Policy had been put into force. Now, my hon. friend from Westmoreland quoted from an election card which was issued by Sir John Thompson, -ini February, 1891, when he was appealing to the electors of the -county of Antigonish, in the province of Nova Scotia. .Sir John Thompson was not an ordinary member of the House, he was Minister of Justice in the government led by Sir John A. Macdonald, and he was recognized as Mr. GOODEVE.
the second in command next to the great Conservative leader. Sir John Thompson was a man in whose judgment the people of Canada had very great confidence. He had occupied a .position on the bench of the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia, and was recognized as one of the 'ablest lawyers in Canada. After the death of Sir John A. Macdonald, he was called upon to assume the leadership of the -Conservative party, which he did with credit to the party and with credit to the country. Every Cana-dan, whether Liberal or Conservative, deplored his s-udden demise at so early an age. Sir John Thompson, in his manifesto, made reciprocity the only question upon which he appealed to the people of Nova Scotia, it is the only great subject to which he refers. He tells the people of Canada, that the government of which he is a member have entered into negotiations with the government at Washington for the purpose of bringing about a treaty of reciprocity, which he believes would be of advantage to the people of both countries. Now, surely the hon. member for Kootenay must have forgotten this fact when he said that the Conservative party was never in favour of reciprocity Subsequent to the adoption of the National Policy. He has forgotten the election of 1891, when the government went to the country upon the policy of reciprocity. My hon. friend has called attention to a portion of the language of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), which will be found on page 60 and following of ' Hansard,' and in which that hon. gentleman, then a member of the Conservative government, stated that this government had done everything possible to extend interprovincial trade, he referred to the fact that the Canadian Pacific railway had been carried out by the Conservative party, and it had then been completed some six years, because it was completed from the Atlantic to the Pacific in 1885. He referred to the enormous- development which had taken place in this country, and said that notwithstanding the development of internal trade, notwithstanding the wonderful strides Canada had made as a result of the construction of the Candian Pacific railway -and the inauguration of the National Policy, yet th-e gov-e-mment had sought to widen and extend the bounds of commerce in every direction. Then he asked this question: With the United States? Yes he says, we are desirous, not only of extending our commerce with all the other countries of the world, but with the United States as well. He refers with pride to the fact that for many years the Conservative party had been taught to watch and to wait until a favourable opportunity- should occur, and he referred gladly to the fact that at last the moment had come when the government had been invited to visit Washing-

ton and to open negotiations with Secretary Blaine and the President of the United States, to bring about what? To bring about a treaty of reciprocity, based upon what? Based upon the .old reciprocity treaty of 1854, with such additions and extensions as the altered circumstances might show to be to the mutual advantage of the two countries.
Surely in the face of this evidence it cannot be said that the Conservative party had abandoned the policy of reciprocity after the introduction of the National Policy. This shows that upon the very last occasion when the Conservative party successfully appealed to the country they made reciprocity the principal plank in their platform, and it was upon that that they hoped to wrin, and did win, the approval of the people.
The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) said more than has been quoted by the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson). He said at page 60:
The government showed itself consistent, in the first place, by declaring that there was a door open for negotiations, and that a delegation would be sent to Washington after the 4th March, and, furthermore, by sending a delegation and being prepared to "go again on the 12th October to do what no Canadian government has been e.sked to do from 1866 to the present time, that is, to talk over the trade matters and relations existing between this country and the United States, with a view to their better and final settlement. This statement which I make will he borne out by the papers, and I cannot see where we have been inconsistent or where we have prejudiced the intersts of Canada

And will hon. gentlemen mark these words:
-or have done aright which any government in favour of reciprocity ought not to have done.
There is the declaration of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) in 1891, after the general elections of that year, showing that the government of which he was a prominent member was in favour of reciprocity with the United States. That course is entirely consistent with what the government had previously done because we find that prior to the election of 1891 and as early as December of 1910 the government passed an order in council in which it was provided that commissioners should go to Washington. And what were to be their instructions? They were to go to Washington with authority, without limitation, to make proposals towards the agreement for a treaty based upon the reciprocity treaty of 1854. I think it is important to bear in mind that they were not to be limited in their instructions, 317i
they were to, if possible, obtain a treaty for reciprocity not in natural products alone -it was'to be based upon the old reciprocity treaty of 1854. But so anxious was the government of that day to obtain better trade relations with the United States, so much did they believe that it would be in the interests of the whole country that this arrangement should be made, that they placed no limitation upon the authority which was to be given to the commissioners, they were given authority to deal with these matters without limitation and perhaps there are some hon. gentlemen here who can remember seeing in the press of that day some remarks that were made as to what was the difference between the Liberal policy of that time of unrestricted reciprocity and the policy of the Conservative party in making an unrestricted offer of reciprocity to the United States. Sir Charles Tupper's attention was called to the fact that these commissioners were to go without limitation to negotiate a reciprocity treaty. Sir Charles Tupper said that was an unrestricted offer of reciprocity, whereas the Liberal party was in favour of unrestricted reciprocity, and Sir Charles said that he pitied the man who could not understand the difference between an unrestricted offer of reciprocity and an offer of unrestricted reciprocity. To the ordinary mind there is not much difference.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: Was the policy of the two parties the same in 1891?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: In 1891 the policy of the Liberal party was broader, it was to include manufactured articles.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: Which was right? '

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext:
It is not necessary to say which was right, because the arrangement which has been made to-day is absolutely in accordance with the limited reciprocity treaty of which the Conservative party was in favour. If my hon. friend will read the speeches which Sir John Macdonald made in discussing this question, he will find that Sir John, while stating that the old reciprocity treaty had been a great benefit to Canada, while stating that no argument need be presented to show that and at the same time saying it- was unfortunately discontinued by the United States government owing to a not unnatural irritation against England, he said that he felt it would be but little use to go to the United States then and seek a, reciprocity treaty. He also intimated that he would be prepared to go even beyond reciprocity in natural products and to give considerable reciprocity in manufactured articles, for the purpose of obtaining reciprocal trade arrangements so far as natural products were concerned.

I would quote from another hon. gentleman whose loyalty I think will not' be impugned in this House, because, although hon. gentlemen who are in the House today, members of the Conservative party, seem, so far as reciprocity is concerned, to have departed from the views of their old and their great leaders of the past, yet I hardly think they would impeach the loyalty of the hon. gentleman from whom I am now going to quote. I refer to the Honourable Sir Charles Tupper, who was for so many years a prominent member of this parliament, and who, for such a long period occupied a prominent position among the people of Canada. I find that Sir Charles Tupper, after the election of 1891, on the 4th of August, as reported at page 3346 of Hansard, said:
The chief point now is, without any quibbling or cavilling, that this government has arranged for a conference with the United States government in October next, without any confession such as hon. gentlemen opposite insinuate, that we are in any sense more dependent upon the satisfactory arrangements tliau are the people of the United States themselves. We go there, relatively, in as strong a position as they meet us; we go there

Willing to negotiate a reciprocity treaty, does he say? No, he says:
We go there anxious" to see whether an arrangement, consistent with the interest of both countries, can be brought about.
And yet to-day hon. gentlemen say that the man who is in favour of reciprocity with the United States is doing something which will imperil the position of Canada as- a portion of the British Empire. They say that the man who is willing to improve the trade relations between this country and the great republic to the south is doing what in fact is an act of disloyalty to the empire because it will tend to draw this country away from 'the great empire to which we are proud to belong, from that great federation of nations which all of us hope and which all the people of Canada believe and hope will for ever remain united and he for ever in the van of progress and development and will last until the end of time. And yet, because this government has simply done what Sir Charles Tupper tried to do, what the hon. Mr. Foster tried to do, what all the eminent statesmen of the past upon both sides of politics tried to do, hon. gentlemen insinuate that they are willing to do something which will weaken the ties that bind Canada to the mother land.
I wish to quote something further, and this perhaps will be of more interest than the remarks which I have quoted, to the people of my own province.
There was not only the order in council providing for the appointment of commis-Hr. PUGSLEY.
sioners, but after the general election in 1891 the speech from the Throne at the opening of parliament contained " the following clause:
*My advisers, availing themselves of opportunities which were presented in the closing months of [DOT] last year, caused the administration of . the United States to be reminded of the willingness of the government of Canada to join in making efforts for the extension and development of the trade between the Republic and the Dominion, as well as for the friendly adjustment of those matters of an international character which remain unsettled. I am pleased to say that these representations have resulted in an assurance that, in October next, the government of the United States will be prepared to enter on a conference to consider the best means of arriving at a practical solution of these important questions. The papers relating to this subject will be laid before you.
The reply to the speech from the Throne was moved by the then member for St. John (Mr. Hazen) who is now the leader of the Conservative government in New Brunswick, and Mr. Hazen then used language which-if we . did not know it was used by one of these younger Conservatives who have departed from the paths trodden by their leaders not very many years ago,- one would think was the language of a supporter of the Liberal party. His speech will be found at p. 8 and following of 'Hansard' 1891, and in it he expressed pleasure as the representative of the city and county of St. John, and as a member of the Conservative party, at the announcement made by the government that they were about to enter into negotiations for a reciprocity treaty with the United States. He went on to speak of the business and social relations existing between the people of Canada and of the neighbouring republic, he expressed the opinion that it would be an advantage to both countries if a reciprocity treaty went into effect, and he concluded by saying that he telt sure it would be gratifying to the people of Canada irrespective of party that steps were about to be taken to secure reciprocity. Nobody will charge that, these Conservatives were any less loyal than the men who now lead the Conservative party; no one will venture to suggest that these Conservatives were less mindful of the best Interests of Canada than those who now lead the party; no one will suggest that they would negotiate for a reciprocity treaty which they thought would have a tendency to draw Canada away from her allegiance to the mother country. But, these gentlemen opposite say to us: the times have changed, and what might be good for Canada in 1891 is not good for Canada to-day. Surely that argument does not apply to the contention that reciprocity is apt to lead tojJismember-ment of the empire; surely, if "to increase

our trade with the United States is likely to weaken our attachment to the mother country to-day, it must have had the same effect 20 years ago. Nay, Sir, there was greater danger of that 20 years ago because while *Canada had then entered upon a stage of development, Canada was not so prosperous as she is to-day, and her people were not in such a position of self-reliance then as they are now. Since then, the population of Canada has increased, her resources have been developed, her trade has extended, and to-day our people are far more powerful than they then were and far better able to stand for what they believe to be the true interests of Canada and the empire. A few words as to the benefit which I believe will accrue to the maritime provinces from this arrangement. We in the lower provinces are very greatly interested in the lumbering, the agricultural, and the fishing industries. We have a great many fertile valleys where vast quantities of hay are produced, and to many farmers it would be a great advantage to sell at least a part of their hay product where they can find a good market. They have looked in the past to the United States but they have been met with a duty of $4 per ton on their hay, and there will be found on file, letters from producers of hay in New Brunswick and Quebec urging the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Customs then negotiating for this arrangement to secure a reduction of at least two dollars per ton in the duty on hay. It was pointed out that many farmers in these provinces would derive great benefit from such a reduction. Well, instead of getting the duty reduced by $2 per ton, the Canadian representatives succeeded in getting the entire duty wiped out and Canadian hay admitted absolutely free of duty to the American market. In the St. John river counties there is a very considerable production of potatoes, and were the duty removed the farmers of these counties would find in the United States an excellent market for their potatoes. It is a fact I believe that during the present generation there have only been two occasions, and then because of crop failures in Canada, when the price of potatoes in the United States has not been higher than the price in New Brunswick. We have very striking evidence of that in the fact that across the border opposite the counties of Carleton and Victoria, in ths county of Aroostook in Maine, farms are today worth on the average about twice as much as farms of equal fertility on the New Brunswick side. A short time ago I made special inquiry in the county of Victoria, and the statements in this respect made some weeks ago in' this House by the hon. member for Carleton were verified by statements made to me by a number of
farmers. And so it is with other farm products. Make farm products of every kind absolutely free of duty, and there will be a large and profitable market for our farmers in the large cities of the New England states, and this they say, would add very greatly to the prosperity of our farmers.
Then, there is another very important in terest in "which our people are deeply <* m-cerned. If hon. gentlemen will look at the papers which are on file, they will find letters from gentlemen largely engaged in the lumbering business, in which they urge that, in .addition to trying to get the United States to take the duty off lumber, they should also try to induce them to Teduce the duty on shingles, which is now 50 cents a thousand, down to 30 cents. And these representations are not confined to lumber manufacturers of the province of New Brunswick, they also come from lumber manufacturers of the province of Quebec-and tha province of British Columbia. They report that the duty, which was raised' by the Paine-Aldrich tariff from 30 cents a thousand to 50 cents, is very nearly prohibitive. I call to mind a letter from a large manufacturer of the province of British Columbia, who stated that, as a result of this change, quite a number of shingle mills in that province were idle; -and I think Representations we)re| made from Nova Scotia as well as from Quebec, that it would seriously cripple the industry in that section of Canada. There is no duty on shingles coming into Canada. I remember that imy hon. friend from the city of Vancouver (Mr. Cowan) went down to the city of Fredericton to enlighten the people there. That city happens to he the centre of quite a large lumber manufacturing inindustry, and he pointed out in all seriousness that as a result of this reciprocity arrangement cedar logs would be sent from New Brunswick into the state of Maine, manufactured- into shingles and brought back to New Brunswick, where they would swamp the shingle market. My hon. friend did not know that for many years shingles had been admitted into Canada free of duty, and under this agreement the only concession made, is made by the United States, which is reducing the duty from 50 cents to 30 cents a thousand. Before the duty was raised to 50 cents, the shipment of shingles to the United States was a considerable factor in the prosperity of that section of Canada; and on the file there will be found a letter from the hon. member for York (Mr. Crocket), who, I believe, has been going from platform to platform warning the people of that loyal county against agreeing to this arrangement, because it will tend to sap the loyalty of the people of Canada. That letter is addressed to the hon. Mr. Fielding, and

in it the hen. member for York says that he has received a communication from a very large lumber manufacturing company which does business in his constituency, and which carries on - operations in some three lumber mills, calling 'attention to the increase which has been made by the United States in the duty on shingles from 30 cents to 50 cents a thousand, and expressing the hope that in any negotiations for the reduction of the tariff between the two countries the Finance Minister will succeed in having the duty reduced.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: Read the letter.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: If I had the file here, I would be glad to do it.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: I understood that the hon. member for York, in this House, denied that statement.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: What did the hon. member for York say?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: He denied that he was giving expression to his own opinion. He was simply communicating to the Finance Minister a letter from one of his constituents.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: I have read the letter, iand any one reading it would take it ais an assurance from the hon. member for York that in forwarding it lie was entirely in accord with the sentiments expressed therein. If the hon. member for York thought that the entering into such an arrangement with the United States would tend to sap the loyalty of the people of Canada, it is a wonder that he did not say to the Minister of Finance: ' While I forward this plea on behalf of one of my constituents, yet I warn you, Mr. Fielding, that if you get the duty on shingles 'removed, so that these lumbermen will be able to send their shingles freely into the United States, it may tend to make them disloyal citizens; it is a very dangerous thing, and you ought to consider it most carefully before you get the United States government to reduce the duty on shingles from 50 cents to 30 cents a thousand.' The hon. membeT for York did not do anything of the kind.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: Will the hon. minister be good enough to point out where any one on this side of the House has ever objected to the United States reducing the duty on wheat or shingles, or on any other commodity going into that country, or where we have ever raised any objection to their managing their own affairs in their own way?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: It has been .stated in this House over and over again that it would be a dangerous thing for us to encourage the United- States government to taxe off the duty on natural products, because it would enable the United States manufacturers to draw from Canada its natural resources and take them into the United States and there .manufacture the goods which ought to be manufactured in Canada; forgetting, of course, that the United States could do that to-morrow7 without any arrangement if it wanted to. All that the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Customs have done by this arrangement has been to sit down quietly with representatives of the United States government and say: Let us talk over what would be to the mutual interest of Canada and the United States to do in the way of reductions of duty. They have made no agreement which binds the people of this country for a single day after this arrangement goes into effect. They declare that this country shall foe absolutely free to make any change in its tariff on the items affected by this arrangement at any time; and while they express the hope that it will be found .so advantageous to the people of both countries that it will be continued for a considerable time, they both take pains to make it absolutely clear that they do not undertake to bind either the Congress of the United States on the one hand or the parliament of Canada on the other. Now, take the matter of lumber. Shall I say my eloquent friend-my interesting friend? Because when the hon. gentleman gets towards the rear part of the chamber, where there are many empty seats at times, and where he can move back and forth and give full vent to his eloquence, he certainly does become exceedingly eloquent. My hon. friend told the people at Fredericton; lumbermen who knew very well the nonsense he was talking-if he will pardon the word-he told these people that under this reciprocity arrangement our lumber would be taken into the United States, manufactured there, and sent back into Canada to compete here with the lumber manufacturers) of New Brunswick. My hon. friend forgot that for many years sawn lumber has been admitted into Canada free of duty.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: Before leaving that point I would like to say I was present and heard the hon. metnber for Vancouver (Mr. Cowan) when dealing with the question of shingles say that their tariff is only reduced back to the old figures whereas shingles coming into Canada are free.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: Shingles are not made free under this arrangement. Shingles have been free for years, and we are making no reduction.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: That is what we object to. They hold them at 30 cents. Whereas shingles coming into this country are free.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext:
That is because we prefer it that way. It has been so for several years, and it has been admitted in the interest of Canada that shingles should be free. I presume it is because the shingle interests in this country do not require any protection as against the United States. At all events I have never heard any suggestion that there should be a duty placed ujjon shingles, so far as Canada is concerned.
For reasons which have appealed to the government lumber has been free. There have been suggestions made at different times in regard to putting a duty upon it, but these suggestions have been very seriously opposed by consumers in Canada, and more particularly by those who live on the prairies, to whom cheap lumber is a most desirable thing. Lumber is made free under this arrangement, but the whole concession is on the part of the United States, and when you bear in mind the fact that the lumbering industry is a very important interest in the maritime provinces, you will agree with me that this is a very important concession, not only for the maritime provinces, but for all sections of Canada. It is of great importance to the province of Ontario-it is of great importance to the Ottawa valley, and it certainly is of great importance to British Columbia, because manufacturers of lumber in these provinces find a large market in the United States for their products. If hon. gentlemen will look at the blue-book they will find the exports of lumber and its products from Canada to the United States for the year ending March 31, 1910, amounted to $22,000,000.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: What were the imports?	.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: I do not know what the imports were. At the moment I am only dealing with the exports because this arrangement will not affect the imports for the simple reason that lumber comes into Canada free to-day.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: What kind of lumber?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: Sawn lumber. And sawn lumber forms a very important part of the lumber exports.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: This treaty makes absolutely no difference in lumber coming into Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: None at all, but it makes a great difference on Canadian lumber going into the United States.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext:
Might I ask the hon. Minister of Public Works if he would allow me to read this letter of Mr. Crocket's:
House of Commons,
Ottawa, March 11, 1910. Honourable W. S. Fielding,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa.
Dear . Mr. Fielding,-I have a communication from the Scott Lumber Company, Ltd., who operate two or three mills in my constituency, requesting me to lay before you, ' n connection with the recent negotiations between the Canadian and tile United States governments upon the tariff matter, the representation that the recent increase in American duty upon shingles has seriously affected the business of Canadian mills, particularly in the maritime provinces. They claim that the rate of 50 cents per thousand is unreasonable and almost prohibitive, and that in the interest of this trade, our government should at least endeavour to have it reduced to the old basis of 30 cents a thousand.
I trust that if the question of revision of the two tariffs is taken up, you will hear this communication in mind.
Yours truly,

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: What does that mean? What the hon. .member for York (Mr. Crocket) does is this-the hon. Minister of Finance is about to enter into negotiations at Washington.. The hon. member for York receives this communication from one of his constituents, calling his attention to the fact that the increase of duty has made importation into the United States prohibitive, and Mr. Crocket expresses^ the hope that the hon. the Finance Minister will bear this communication in mind during the course of the negotiations. This the hon. Finance Minister did. I have no doubt in the world that the hon. member for York was absolutely sincere when he said that it would be in the interest of the manufacturers of this country that the duty should be Teduced, and, as a matter of fact the duty was reduced from 50 cents to 30 cents.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: You misrepresented him before.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: I will not contradict my hon. friend further than to say that his memory does not serve him correctly as to what was said.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext:
Might I ask a question? I would like to ask the hon. minister if in his opinion the following would be true reciprocity? Supposing I, as a manufacturer of shingles at the Canadian Soo send a carload of shingles oyer to the American Soo, and I am met at the border with a duty of 30 cents per 1000 according to the new arrangement, or a duty of 50 cents per 1000 according to the old arrangement; my competitors from the Ameri-

can Soo wish to send a carload of shingles over to the Canadian Soo and pays no duty -is that true reciprocity?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: There is nothing in the arrangement which would prevent Canada from making the duty just the same as in the United States.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: Why don't you do it?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: Because it was never thought to be in the interest of the people of Canada to have a duty on shingles. So far as I know, we have not had a duty on shingles for years and years, if we ever had. So it is with regard to sawn lumber -we have no duty on that article. The United States had a duty of $1,25 a thousand, and thev have thrown off that duty entirely; the concession is wholly on the part of the United States, for Canada in that respect makes no concession.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: I desire to ask the hon. gentleman a question. The United States took off the duty of ,$1.25 on lumber and made it free, because they have a surplus. But we can supply them with shingles and they put on a duty of 30 cents. Why do they not make shingles free.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: All that the shingle manufacturer's of British Columbia asked was that the duty be reduced to 30 cents, it having been raised from 30 cents to 50 cents.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: I desire to correct the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley); I happen to know that that is not correct. What the shingle mill men want is an exact equality of tariff.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext:
I can only say that I have read the files showing the petitions from the shingle manufacturers' association in British Columbia, and all they asked for is that the duty shall be reduced from 50 cents under the Payne-Aldrich tariff to 30 cents as it was previously, and that concession was obtained by the commissioners on behalf of Canada. The matter of removing the duty on lumber is of great importance to the people of New Brunswick, especially to the people of St. John. We have had in force in the United States for sixty years past what is known as the Pike law. Under that* law timber could be cut in the forests of northern Maine by American citizens, floated down the river St. John to the city of St. John, manufactured there in American mills by American citizens and shipped into the United States free of duty. I think I can safely say that that has been of enormous bentfit to the port of St. John. These mills have given employment to many hundreds of men. They have given employment also Mr. GORDON (Nipissing).
to many coasting vessels in taking the lumber from the port of St.John to the ports of the United States. Under the Payne-Aldrich tariff that law was repealed and on the fifth of next month that repeal comes into effect.
Therefore, this privilege will be denied to the American citizens who are living in the city of St. John and are manufacturing their lumber there. The result will be that they will have to pay on lumber going into-the United States $1.25 a thousand. I am told that, in view of the very large stump-age they have to pay to the land owner in Northern Maine and the large expense in floating the logs down to the port of St. John, this duty of $1,25 will be prohibitive-and in all human probability these mills will have to close. If, however, the proposed arrangement comes into effect, lumber manufactured in Canada will go into the United States free of duty and these industries will be continued. So far as that branch of the lumber business is concerned, it is of very great importance to the people of the city of St.John. I think the same remark applies to a lesser extent to the St. Croix river which is also-affected by the Pike law'.
Now, with regard to this question of loyalty: I cannot understand how the loyalty of our people can in any way be affected by this arrangement except in the effect it will have upon people who will be benefited by the reciprocal arr'angemetnt. The lumber manufacturers are going to be benefited. Are they going to become less loyal to the Empire by reason of this? The hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Gorden). I believe, ships lumber to the United States. Possibly he will not deny that he ships almost his entire output to that country.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: I do not.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: At any rate that is the destination of a considerable part of his output. Under this reciprocal arrangement he will be able to ship a larger quantity than at present. That is not going to affect his loyalty. I venture to say that if his lumber output were increased tenfold he would be as loyal a citizen of Canada as ever and would fight for the old flag and teach his children to love the empire just as much as he does today. It is not going to affect the loyalty of the people simply because thev ship more lumber to the United States.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: Will that make it, cheaper in Canada?

speechtext:

speechtext: When this arrangement comes into effect, how will it affect the consumers of lumber in this country?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: So far as the province of New Brunswick is concerned, and I believe the same remark applies to other sections of Canada, there is plenty of lumber for the consumers of Canada, and plenty of lumber to send abroad; and if the lumber is properly taken care of, that will be the case for generations to come.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: I was not concerned about the quantity of lumber, I was concerned about the price the consumer will have to pay.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, 1 would not object at ail if the price of the natural product should be increased. I would not object if the farmer got more for . his product, I would not object if the lumber manufacturer got more for his product,, provided he shared it with the labouring man who helps to make his profit. Kor myself, I would not care if I had to pay more for it. I think it will be to the benefit of this country if the wages of the labouring men are increased, and if the labour of the farmer, the fisherman, the miner and the lumberman shall be better recompensed than it is to-day. I do not think that in this country, labour receives, or has received, its fair proportion of benefits from the wonderful development and progress which has taken place in Canada during the last 15 years. As a result of this development we have seen many people grow in wealth from being comfortable to becoming millionaires. And while the wages of the labouring men have increased, I do not think they have increased to the proportion I would like to see them increase. I trust that as a result of this arrangement, and as a result of the increased profits which will come to the farmer, the lumberman 'and the fisherman, the labouring men who are employed in helping to make those profits will receive their fair share of the increased benefit, as I think they ought to do. *
Now, a few words more, and I will not detain the House further. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition, when he was in the west, said I want it understood that I am unalterably opposed to this arrangement, and I am opposed to it, 1 thmlc he said, principally because it will tend to i draw Canada away from her allegiance to ; the British Crown, and draw her gradually i I into commercial,, if not political union
100S7

with the United States. I think that was about what he said, judging from what 1 saw in the newspapers. Now, my hon. friend the Prime Minister said, That is all nonsense. I think there should be an adjective put before the word ' nonsense.' It does seem to .me. difficult to understand how men can put forward such an absurd proposition as that-to say that because the people of this country can be given a wider market, because they can be given greater facilities for trade with the United States, their loyalty will be weakened, that they will be drawn away from the British Empire. I say that does seem to me a proposition _ too absurd to consider seriously. Why, Sir, if that were so, would Canada not be less loyal to-day than she was 15 years ago? Fifteen years ago what was the trade between Canada and the United States? It certainly was not over $150,000,000 or $200,000,000, at the outside. What is it to-day? According to the trade and navigation returns for the year which closed on the 31st of March lust, our trade with the United States amounted to the enormous sum of $404,000,000.
An lion. MEMBER. Mostly imports.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext:
What does that show? It shows that our people are trading with the United States to a vastly larger extent than they were fifteen years ago; I do not care whether the trade is in imports or exports. Our commercial relations with them are becoming more intimate, because a larger number of people are trading with the people of the United States than there were fifteen years ago. Now are we less loyal to-day than we were then? I think not. I think there never was a time in the history of Canada when the people were more loyal to the empire than they are to-day, when the young men of Canada were so ready to" sacrifice their blood in defence of the old flag as they arc to-day. But an hon. gentleman opposite says that our trade -with the United States is mostly imports. Well, it is true. The imports were $285,000,000, and the exports were $119,000,000. Now, Sir, hon. gentlemen speak of trade gcing north and south. Do they bear in mind that this trade wnich we have today with the United States is more than one-half of the whole trade which Canada carries on with the entire world, that mote than one-half of our total trade to-day is with the United States? Surely that must be trade going north and south. The hon. gentleman says it is mostly imports. Of course it is. Our imports are double what the exports are. What does that mean? It means that we are bringing north into Canada $285,000,000 worth of goods, and we are sending south into the United States $119,000,000 worth. Is it desir-Mr. PUGSLEY.
able that that state of affairs should continue? What does it mean? It means that we are paying to the United States the gold which we draw from other countries of the world for exports that we sell to them. Would it not be to the advantage of the Canadian people that we should sell to the United States, at all events, as much as we import from them? I think it would. If we find it in our own interest to import $285,000,000 worth of goods from the United States, goods coming by train and by steamer, surely if we can send goods back in return we accomplish a two-fold object, we make it more profitable for the transportation companies who will have return freights, and, therefore, the rates ought to be reduced so that we shall get our imports to the people at a cheaper rate than at present, and it would accomplish the other purpose, that we would pay by the products of Canada for the goods which we buy from the United States, instead of _ being obliged to send our gold there which we draw from the other countries of the world.
_ No one can deny that it wou'd be to The interests of Canada that we should at least send to the United States as much as we import from them, but, as I have said, the larger trade which has grown up during these years has not in any way affected the loyalty of the people of Canada and I am one of those who firmly believe that it will be to the interests of the people of the whole of Canada that we should get larger markets for the products of our farms, our forests, our mines and our fisheries. I know that down in the province of New Brunswick we have fisheries of very great importance, of enormous value; they are handicapped bv the duty which the United States have imposed upon them. If that duty were removed it would greatly add to the profits of the fishermen. Hon. gentlemen may say that that will not be to the interest of those who consume fish in Canada, I say it will make but little difference in the price of fish; but even if it does we should be willing when we can get it so easily, to confer this small benefit upon the hardy fishermen of our country, we should remove this handicap from them, and enable them to carry on their business at a greater profit than to-day. They endure great hardships, what little they earn they earn in the hardest possible way and in the face of the great possible dangers, and any thing we can do to encourage the hardy fishermen along our coasts, to make their industry more successful and to produce greater profit to them, we ought to do most cheerfully.

The firm of Davidson & McRae, of New Westminster. I have been at their mill, which is one of the largest on the continent of America, and I believe they operate several mills giving employment at the woods and at their various mills to a good many thousand people. I have the authority of a member of that firm for the statement that in all probability, if this arrangement goes into effect, they will find a very profitable market in San Francisco and other cities upon the western coast of the United States for their lumber and that it will mean in all human probability an added profit of about $1 per thousand upon the output of their mills.
I was also informed that the removal of the American duty on fish oil will result in a profit to one of the big fishing companies being established upon the Canadian Pacific coast of somewhere in the vicinity of $200,000 a year. These are only samples of industries which are going to be affected
by this arrangement. I use the name of these large manufacturers of lumber with their authority. They did not give me the information in confidence but gave me authority to use their name in respect to this arrangement and the advantage that would accrue to the lumbering interests.
Therefore, believing as I do that this, arrangement will be greatly to the interest of the producers of Canada, to the great toiling masses of the people who are represented by the farmers, the fishermen, the lumbermen and the miners, I do, not see how any one who really has the best interests of this country at heart can oppose this arrangement.
Honourable gentlemen opposite have intimated this afternoon very plainly that they intend to exercise their prerogative as members of this House to prevent this question coming to a vote. They intimated that as plainly as words can intimate any thing. In the British parliament it was found necessary to take a course which was approved of by both the political parties to prevent useless discussion and to prevent a minority from taking such a course as would prevent the transaction of the ordinary business of parliament. That course was taken and had to be taken in the British parliament; that course was taken and had to be taken in the American House of representatives. It has been assumed by those who have had control of this parliament in the past that gentlemen who come here would recognize that it was their duty to have a full and a thorough discussion upon all questions which are brought before parliament. It was believed that would be the case, but it was also believed that when the time necessary for that full and free discussion had passed, gentlemen would allow a vote to be taken and allow the will of the majority to prevail until at all events the people had an opportunity of passing upon their conduct and upon the conduct of the majority. The threats which hon. gentlemen have made this afternoon tend towards almost if not quite revolutionizing the theory which has hitherto prevailed. That theory has been that gentlemen would recognize not only their rights but their duty and that is that the will of the majority shall prevail. That is recognized throughout this country as governing all assemblies, all meetings in which people are concerned, and at any meeting attended by the people of this country, whenever there has been fair and reasonable opportunity for the discussion of any question, the minority have always recognized that the view of the majority shall prevail so far at all events as that body is concerned; and so in this parliament I ask hon. gentlemen opposite whether, after hon. gentlemen have had a full

opportunity, as they have had during the time that this question has been under discussion, of expressing their views, it is not tending to destroy free parliamentary institutions for hon. gentlemen to rise as they have risen to-day and threaten that this question shall not be allowed to come to a vote until the people have passed upon it.

speechtext: What about 1896?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: I don't care what took place in 1896; I was not here in 1896. I say it is not in harmony with the principles which ought to govern parliamentary institutions that gentlemen should rise in their places and threaten, simply because their views are not the views of the majority, that there shall be no opportunity to vote upon this question, and no opportunity, in a constitutional way, of giving expressions to the views of the majority of the members of this House. That is revolutionary; it is not in harmony with the principles of constitutional government. And if as a result of the obstruction of these gentlemen; if, as a result of their threats, there shall be no opportunity of having the votes of the members of this House recorded; if it shall be necessary to consult the people before the time they ordinarily would be consulted, I venture to say that the people of this Dominion will express their opinion favourable to the government, not only with reference to this great question, which is before parliament and the people of the country, but also with reference to the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite, who although in a minority are seeking by abuse of the constitutional rules of this House to prevent the view of the majority from prevailing.

Mr. Speaker, I have not charged the Minister of Finance with any such attempt. I say that he has given this afternoon another honourable instance of his veracity. Again, when he told the House to-day' that he proposed to throttle and gag the will of the people and to go to the country without redistribution, he declared an intention to perpetrate the blackest injustice on western Canada that any public man ever attempted. For my own part I represent a constituency whose population is two per cent, of the whole of Canada. If my constituency were taken as the basis of representation of the House instead of 221 indifferent looking members here there would be less than fifty. I represent as many people as five ordinary members like the Minister of Public Works. Will the Minister of Finance dare to tell the people of my constituency that they should have only one voice in the councils of the country instead of the four or five they are entitled to, and on a question that reverses the policy which Canada has followed with success for the last forty-five years? Will the Minister of Finance dare to come into my constituency and tell the people that he will deprive them of their franchise and of their full voice on a question which concerns not only their future prosperity, but the destiny of Canada per se and of Canada as a part of the British Empire? If that Minister of Finance dares to come into my constituency I undertake that I will compel his candidate to lose his deposit. I am in one respect delighted to find that my appeal to the House two evenings ago has been effective.
It may be that the gentleman to whom I appealed for assistance added their efforts to mine and convinced this govern-

ment that in these dog days this is no proper place for them, that their proper place is before the people of this country giving an account of their stewardship, giving some reason for the faith that is in them that this reciprocity thing i>s going to advantage any part of the people of Canada, It may be, I say, thay my appeal to the yonnger members of the government has been effective. It may be that, without an appeal 'to the Minister of Public Works, he has added his influence to that of the other younger members of the cabinet to induce the government to do its duty. I did not appeal the other evening to the Minister of Public Works. I recognized that the appeal to him would need to be of a different kind from the appeal which I made to the other ministers. The other evening, when I made that appeal, we were discussing the patented device by which the Liberals of Vancouver diverted from the coffers of the Dominion treasury into their own pockets no less than a million dollars. T was not sure at that time that that diversion would awaken in the breast of the Minister of Public Works that horror which I felt it might awaken in the breasts of the other members of the government. That sum is so far beyond $135,000 that I was not sure but that instead of horror at a moral outrage, it might be chagrin and envy that I would awaken in
his breast.
But IbefoTe I to the speech Public Works, that interesting the hon. member (Mr. Eimmerson) to
refer more particularly of the Minister of I wish to refer to effort on the part of for Westmorland uncover the mossgrown tombs of 1854. With Rip Van Winkle wisdom he went back to 1854 tas if the conditions of to-day were the conditions of that time, and he is going still. He has evidently forgotten that this is 1911 instead of 1854. To do more than make that short reference would be, I think, a mistake. Apart altogether from the waste of ammunition, there is but little sport in shooting at a dead goose.
I come now to the benign, the complacent Minister of Public Works. The Minister of Public Works, feeling the sting that resulted from my shoTt trip throuph New Brunswick, has come into the House and attempted to distort my statements made on the public platforms of that province.
