I agree, Mr. Speaker, that it does not correctly describe the minister's attempt. In New Brunswick I was endeavouring to point out the effect of this reciprocity pact. You know that they call it a pact. They say it is not a treaty, it
is not a convention; the most they will allow us to call it is a pact, and I sometimes think that is an appropriate name. It is packed -full of all sorts of misfortunes and evil for Canada. In New Brunswick I was pointing out to the people of New Brunswick that men like the Minister of Public Works and men like the artist in truth who spoke this afternoon, .are declaring to the people of Canada that in the main essentials this is a renewal of the old treaty of 1854, with the accent On the old; and, Mr. Speaker, there is a great deal of truth in their statement. That old treaty, like this new treaty, does this. They both place natural products on the free list; but while they do that, they leave the tariff on goods not covered by the treaty twice * as high, or almost twice as high, when entering the United States as when entering Canada. For example, under the old treaty of 1854 the average American tariff was 24 per cent, while the average Canadian tariff was 101.
Again at the present time the average American tariff is 46 per cent, while the average Canadian tariff is 24 per cent. I would point out to the good people of New Brunswick, as I venture to point out to this House, that as long as that inequality obtains between the tariff of the United States, and the tariff of Canada, so long will the effect of that treaty be to transfer the manufacturing business	and the
carrying trade of Canada from Canada to the United States.	I pointed out in New Brunswick, and I wish to point out here, that our experience under the old treaty was that while the natural products of Canada flooded into the United States, the manufactured products of Canada were walled out of the United States by a high prohibitive tariff, but at the same time the American manufactured goods were flooding into Canada over the Canadian tariff walls like a gushing toTrent from the mountainside.
I think I can almost repeat the idea I expressed there. I pointed out that it was no time for Canada to enter into a treaty of this kind with the United States, and
that the time would not come for Canada to enter into such a treaty until the United States brought their tariff to a level with the tariff of Canada on all products. I mentioned the case of shingles; and let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I am not oblivious to the fact that shingles have been admitted free into Canada since the session of 1898. At the tail end of that session, when many of the members had gone home, and when interest in legislation had dwindled, a provision was sneaked through this House that American shingles should enter Canada free. Ever since that I know very well that American shingles have been coming

into Canada free, while Canadian shingles have been going into the United States by jumping a tariff wall, of 30 cents a 1000 at first and later of 50 cents per 1000.
If I might be permitted, Mr. Speaker, to disturb the peaceful slumbers of the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue, I would point out to him that if he could spare a few wakeful moments to the consideration of this question, he would find that the article in the ' Daily Times ' of Victoria, under date July 12, is a little off colour in regard to the facts. In that article he says: ' It is our duty to point out that it is not a part of the proposal under the reciprocity agreement to allow American made shingles to enter Canada free.' The profundity of that article, and the wisdom displayed in it is well nigh beyond comprehension, especially in view of the fact that at page 20 of the official document setting forth the terms of this agreement between Canada and the United States, item number 502, it appears that shingles are to enter Canada free. The Minister of Inland Revenue is out in his statement merely by the omission of the word ' not ' in this editorial or leader in the paper owned and edited by him. So that the hon. minister is a little wrong when he says that American shingles are not to - be admitted into Canada free. Because, as a matter of fact, American shingles are to be admitted into Canada free. When he examines item 502 of the official document, I imagine that, like the good honest man he poses to be, he will see .he has made a mistake, and that this is a discrimination against British Columbia, and that he will come over to our side and oppose this agreement. I knew that shingles have been free since the fall of 1898. I know at the same time that the effect of this agreement on the shingle manufacturers in British Columbia would be to compel them to locate upon the south instead of the north side of the boundary line. Because the reason with which I am endowed told me that the shingle manufacturer would not, for tfie privilege of paying 30 cents a thousand on his output, locate on the north side of the line when by locating .on the south side of the line he could avoid payment of that 30 cents on going into the American market, and still have access to the Canadian market without paying a cent.

Do I understand that the Minister of Public Works abandons his contention with regard to the lumbermen of British Columbia? He was speaking about the lumbermen of British Columbia,
and he dare not in face of that record made by ' Hansard,' deny my statement, he was speaking of the lumbermen of British Columbia. I propose to read the petition to him, and to the other members of the government, to show their opinion in regard to the tariff. That petition, or resolution, reads as follows:
Whereas the coast and mountain lumber manufacturers have repeatedly brought to the attention of the Dominion government, as well as the public generally, the necessity for protection on rough lumber, with the exception of hardwoods; and
Whereas the representations of the lumbermen have bad the endorsation on many occasions of every board of trade in British Columbia, and of the Canadian Manufacturer's Association; and
Whereas it is a matter of common knowledge, which the government can readily verify, that) American lumber manufacturers use Canada as a convenient dumping ground for their sur- * plus low-grade products, which at the present time is being sold in Canada from Washington, Idaho and Montana mills for less than the logs cost British Columbia manufactuers;
Whereas the American market is practically closed to Canadian lumber by reason of the protective tariff maintained by the United States government; and
Whereas the American market is known to be glutted with low-grade lumber, and is likely to he more so in the future, owing to the closer logging of timber limits; and
Whereas the lumber industry is the only industry of any magnitude in Canada not afforded some measure of protection; and
Whereas the lumber industry is the chief industry of British Columbia and its profitable operation in this province is practically made impossible through lack of protection on low-grade lumber;
It is therefore resolved that, in the judgment of the associated hoards of trade of eastern British Columbia, the Dominion government is not only amply justified in placing a duty of $2 per thousand feet on rough lumber, with the exception of hardwoods, but in all fairness should do so forthwith.

If the hon. member were discussing the general question of protection on lumber then outside of this question of reciprocity the resolution would be pertinent to such a discussion, but I say it is not the policy of this government to put higher duties on lumber and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden), speaking for his party, has never said it was the policy of the opposition, and if my hon. friend wishes to convey that the policy of his friend was to meet the wishes of the British Columbia lumbermen and put a higher duty on lumber, I say we have no evidence whatever that that is the policy of the opposition, and if any hon. member of the opposition from the prairie provinces is present he will not agree with the hon. gentleman.

speechtext:
I am prepared to discuss this either in the light or in the darkness of this reciprocity proposal. I want to remind you that in 1894 the Americans put upon their statute books a statutory offer to remove the American duty on rough lumber if Canada would remove the Cana-Mr. FIELDING.
dian duty on rough lumber. In the following year Canada, believing in the good faith of that offer removed the Canadian duty on rough lumber. But the Americans forgot the pledge contained in their statutory offer and did not and have not to this day removed the American duty on lumber. In 1896 a new government came into power in Canada but they did not, as we, on this side of the House had a right to expect, seek to protect the interests of Canada as they should have done by reimposing that Canadian duty on lumber when the Americans made default in their statutory promises. As a result the American lumber came flooding into Canada and the Canadian lumber was barred out of the United States by a prohibitive tariff which they had promised to remove. The Minister of Finance says that under these conditions this resolution that I have read was passed. It was passed, however, under these circumstances, that the people of the West, as well of * the people of the East, knew that the Minister of Finance was chasing after the powers that be at Washington and attenpting to get a reciprocity treaty. But, nevertheless, there may be some virtue in the statement that this resolution which I have read was passed prior to his announcement of the reciprocity proposal.
However, I am fortunate in having under my hand the view of the lumbermen of British Columbia since these reciprocity proposals have been made to the people of Canada. It is the view of the lumbermen of British Columbia voiced by Mr. .7. E. H. Barnet, a lumberman who has made a success of his undertakings in Ottawa as in the West, made on behalf of the lumbermen of British Columbia on July 15, and I would ask the attention of the Minister of Finance to this statement in the hope that even in this eleventh hour.

speechtext:
Even at this hour of 11.25 he may be induced to return from his love and his desire to hand over the fiscal independence and the tariff autonomy of Canada to the people of the United States. Mr. Barnet's statement reads as follows:
' The red, white and blue, with its present number of stars, is sufficient for me, and I am not at all anxious to add another star to our neighbour's flag with my vote,' is the opinion on reciprocity forcefully expressed by Mr. J. E. H. Barnett, who arrived here yesterday from Renfrew, when seen at the Hotel Vancouver.
Though Mr. Barnet's timber interests in this and other provinces are figured in the millions, and since timber men on this side of the boundary line are commonly credited with standing to reap considerable benefit from any prospective reciprocity treaty between Canada and the United States, Mr. Barnet is too loyal to the flag of his own country to permit him-

self to be swayed by sordid selfishness when the prosperity of the entire Dominion is at stake.
To my way of looking at it, this question of reciprocity lightly or altogether in the nature of a commercial agreement, for if such were the case I would soon be found on the side of those advocating it, but a step that is likely to create a chilled feeling between Canada and the mother country. Frankly, I believe the whole scheme is just in keeping with the almost imperial commercial policy of the United States. This reciprocity treaty is simply a bait held out to us in the hope that we will be beguiled into such a trap, under the guise of keeping dangling before our eyes an entry for our products into a market estimated at 90,000,000 inhabitants. But let the too-confident Canadian beware of the wily sons of Uncle Sam, who do not care a rap for our prosperity, but for their own. They are not so philanthropicalfy inclined as to throw their doors wide open to us. What they will take from us is just a drop in a bucket compared to what they expect to ship into our markets. It is an absolute fact that American factories have been increased to such an extent for the past five years that if they want to continue to run at full blast they must find an additional market for their surplus products, as they put out nearly one-third more than the market of their own country can handle.'
In other words, unlike the Minister of Finance, the patriotism of the British Columbian is not measured by the price of a sack of potatoes on the Boston market, or the price of a car of lumber at the Chicago market.
The lumbermen of British Columbia are too intelligent to be fooled by a device of that kind. They realize that while $1.25 per thousand is taken off the lumber duty by the United States the effect of this treaty will he to increase the cost of living for the workingmen of Canada. If you increase the cost of living you diminish the return to labour and you diminish the purchasing power of wages. There are advocates of this reciprocity who maintain that the farmer of Alberta and Saskatchewan will get more for his wheat and cattle, but I remind hon. gentlemen that 80 per cent of the animal and agricultural products of the country are consumed in Canada, and if you increase the price of the 20 per cent sent out of the country you increase the price of the 80 per cent consumed within, and you necessarily increase the cost of living in this country. You lessen the purchasing power of wages and salary and capital; you interfere with that almost perfect equilibrium we have established in Canada between the three great industrial elements, agriculture, commerce, and manufactures, by the national policy adopted in 1878 and in force ever since. That policy has brought about a condition of general prosperity in Canada in which the farmer, and the workingman, and every citizen of the country has had full and fair share.
To disturb that equilibrium is to disturb the prosperity of Canada. Under the reciprocity treaty of 1854, the effect was that the railways and steamboats were busy carrying American manufactured goods into Canada, and return cargoes to the United States of Canadian natural products, not to be consumed in the United States but to be carried by American railways to American ports and thence shipped to the markets of the world. The government of the old provinces of Canada realized that that treaty was destroying the manufacturing industry of this country and handing over the carrying trade to the United States, and in 1860 they imposed a tariff on leather goods, wearing apparel, cotton and woollen goods such as we could manufacture in Canada and with the revenue from that tariff they began to develop railway and canal systems so as to retain the carrying trade whch had been diverted by the treaty of 1854. So soon as the American authorities saw that Canada was adopting that policy, there arose a cry that this was an injustice to the industries and trade of the United States, just as if this treaty is adopted it will arise again if we attempt to change our tariff on any of the articles not covered by the treaty. That cry became so persistent that in 1866 the United States abrogated that reciprocity treaty. And they abrogated that treaty in the hope and belief that it would either drive Canada into the American Union or into bankruptcy. It did neither, but it did develop a crop of secessionists like the Minister of Finance, and a crop of commercial unionists like the whole party that constituted the Liberal opposition of Canada in 1891: a crop of unrestricted reciprocity advocates, a small, demoralized crop at the present day, who form the rump and remnant of the growth of 1866.
But, notwithstanding this crop, Canada had men equal to the situation; men who developed a policy of Canada for Canadians, Canadian development for Canadian labour and Canadian capital, a policy inaugurated in 1878 and in force at the present day. Now it is proposed to reverse that policy, which has developed the home market of Canada, a market able to take care of 80 per cent of the production of Canada. And how great is that production? The yearly production of Canada is greater per head of population than the yearly production of any other country of the known world, and the price which is received for Canada's annual production, in her home market at the door of the producer, is such that it makes the average Canadian a richer man than the citizen of any other nation of Canada's population in the known world. But, Sir, this policy would reverse that. This policy would revert to the old quagmire of 1854. It would



ask us to return to that which in 1854 was a necessity, but which in 1911 would be a curse. How foolish, how fatal to the future o+ Canada is this blind indifference to the fact that this is 1911 and not 1854. When I heard the Minister of Finance in January last expound the policy of Canada in 1854, 1 was reminded of my student days, when 1 studied with peculiar interest the works of Washington Irving, and wondered if our Minister of Finance in Canada to-day was but the reincarnation of Rip Van Winkle. Had he forgotten that fifty-seven, years have expired since 1854, that conditions have changed, that Canada has forged ahead to the very forefront of the commercial nations of the world, that Canada no longer is on the verge of bankruptcy, that her exchequers are no longer crippled, that her people are no longer scattered communities spread in sparse settlements from the Atlantic to the Pacific. I wondered if the Minister of Finance had been asleep for the last 57 years. I wondered if, with the prophetic eye of a seer, Washington Irving had predicted the life and work and experience of a Minister of Finance of Canada. And, again, when I remembered that this is a scheme for transferring the tariff jurisdiction of Canada from Canada to the United States, as the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) declared today, I bethought myself that this may be true. I remembered that the effect of this tieaty was to destroy that which the Premier of Canada, with charming lip-loyalty, has declared to be a cardinal principle with him, British preference. I remembered that the mother land sent to us last year $3,500,000 worth of metals of different kinds, and that the effect of this treaty would be to wipe out and destroy fox ever that British preference. I remembered that the mother land last year sent to us $2,000,000 worth of automobiles, clocks, watches and such goods, and that the effect of this treaty, if ratified, would be to reduce that British preference by at least one-half. But, Mr. Speaker, I remembered that the effect of this treaty would be to establish a new precedent in the history of the British Empire. For the first time one of the members of that empire is bargaining with a foreign country to exclude the rest of the British Empire from the preference which by that bargain this country is getting in that foreign country; in other words, by a bargain with a foreign country, we are agreeing with that country to discriminate and differentiate, not only against the mother land, but against the other parts of the British Empire.
In 1892, James G. Blaine, who was at that time a great power in the United States, made a proposal of that kind to ths Canadian government. The government of that day was a Conservative government, Mr. COWAN.	[DOT]	, ;	!
and they rejected that proposal with scorn, on the ground that it involved a differentiation and a discrimination against the mother land. When I remembered that I was unable to understand why the Prime Minister of Canada should allow these things in favour of a foreign power and discriminate 'against the mother land. But, Sir, the explanation of the attitude of this government and of this premieT is to be found in the declaration of the premier in London, in the month of June, when he said in effect, that we, base Canadians, were mere fair weather members of the British Empire, willing to accept the protection and the benefits that pertained to a member of the British Empire, but unwilling not only to share in the common interest and defence of the empire, but even to take counsel with the other members of the British Empire in regard to that common interest and that common defence.

I might also tell hon. gentlemen that if it be true that we have no market value for certain commodities, we must force these commodities on the markets of the United States, and inasmuch as the United States are willing to rebate the duty it will inure to the benefit of the producer in this country of certain commodities. That seems to me the argument they are using in their press; and yet two hon. gentlemen opposite have stated on the floor of the House that there was no fault to find with the United States remitting their duties. If that be true, what is there 3184
in this arrangement? Is there anything more in it than Canada remitting a portion of the duties that are collected today?

It was my great pleasure to be in this city in 1893 at the convention of the Liberal party, and I can distinctly remember the plank in the platform asking for a tariff for revenue only, and also the plank in favour of reciprocal trade relations with the United States in natural products and in a certain well defind list of manufactured articles. What is this trade arrangement but a fulfilment of the promise made in 1893? We went to the country in 1896 and the country put us in power. And when, in a critical condition of the trade of this country some 12 months ago, when the United States threatened to put on a surtax on our exports going to that country did we not do our duty? It is a thing to be dreaded. The proposed policy of the United States meant that whereas, on the fish we are sending to them they collected duties amounting to $500,000, under the surtax they would have collected another $250,000, out of the pockets of the people of this country for the effect of the surtax; would have been to increase the duty 50 per cent. So, I say, it was in the interest of the country that some_ arrangement should ibe arrived at. And it was arrived at with very little sacrifice on the part of Canada. The principal article on which we made a reduction was cotton seed oil, and I do not think that reduction would hurt any manufacturer in Canada. So, I say, we have carried out the platform of the Liberal .party ladopted

in 1P03, and on which we came into power. In 1396 when this government came into power, the government was collecting from the iionsuming public about $19 for every 'hundred dollars' worth of goods that went thro ;igh the Customs House.
Lu st year we collected about $16 on every hundred dollars' worth, which is a reduction of about 15 per cent. And if this arrangement goes through, it will mean a further reduction of about three per cent- that is, we collect about $70,000,000 through the Customs House and under this arrangement this would 'be reduced by about $2,500,000, which is about three per cent. Yet these hon. gentlemen have the audacity to tell us that we have no mandate, though we are carrying out the platform on which we returned to power and which we have repeated at every election. I admit that the" question of reciprocal trade relations was not a live issue during the last three elections. But it was for the very reason I have already explained- that the Prime Minister had said that overtures in the future must come from the United States. But when those overtures were made we were called upon to act in accordance with the principles laid down by the Liberal party. Nor was this principle confined to the Liberal party, for, in 1894 a law was placed on the statute book making an open offer to the United States of reciprocal trade relations, in fish and certain other natural products. And yet, these hon. gentlemen tell us, forsooth, we have no mandate for reciprocity. It is greatly to the benefit of Canada to have many of these duties removed, because in the articles affected we find a market only in the United States. This is true of a * certain species of our fish-we have no market except the home market and that in the United States. We have practically no market for shingles except in the United States, and the same is true of laths. Inasmuch as we must market these articles there, duty or no duty we say it is a benefit to our people to have free access to this market of 92,000,000 of people. It will be a boon to us when this trade arrangement is finally put into effect.
For the opposite side, I would say that it would be a great calamity to Canada at large and a great calamity to the maritime provinces. I wish to give one or two reasons why I think the position taken by hon. gentlemen opposite is not a logical one. First I shall refer to something said in reference to myself by the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley). That hon. gentleman referred to the hon. member for Argen-teuil (Mr. Perley) as one who would benefit to the extent of $90,000 a year on lumber in the event of this compact going through. Notwithstanding that large financial benefit, when this hon. member opposed this pact the minister went on to impugn his motiyes for doing so. I ventured to suggest that that was a position unworthy of the Minister of Public Works. The hon. gentleman replied that he was not surprised, that such criticism should come from me. It is true I have not won for myself a name such as has the Minister of Public Works. I have not had the privilege nor do I want the privilege of taking part in any sawdust wharf transactions or McAvity deals. I would be perfectly willing for the rest of my life to occupy the humble position I do rather than to find myself in the limelight by such means a?

speechtext:
lie has adopted. I can readily understand that to the Minister of Public Works the matter of an hon. gentleman placing his country and principle ahead of a matter of $90,000 would be something out of the question. We can all understand that would be something entirely foreign to the course he would pursue.
I have been somewhat interested to hear the hon. gentleman refer to Liberal principles. I have here a campaign document circulated very extensively by the Liberal party previous to the last general election, entitled: 'Party government in Canada, a western Liberal view.' Without passing any opinion on the contents in detail I would say it is on the whole very well written. There are one or two expressions in it which I wish to call to the attention of the hon. gentlemen opposite. The writer of this pamphlet referring to responsible government says:
The counting of the ballots on election night decides not only who shall govern during the succeeding parliamentary term but how they shall govern. The election of representatives to parliament is, in effect, a plebiscite or popular vote, rejecting or continuing the line of policy upon which the affairs of government, have, up to that moment, been administered. A general election is a sitting of the highest court of appeal, the court of last resort on all public questions. The decision given takes effect at once and in practice is only reversed at a future election.
Therefore, we have a guiding principle of our system of government that the election of a parliament decides the policy of the party which is to govern. By the proposal introduced by this government, if this reciprocity pact is put through at the present time, it seems to me it is placing the cart before the horse, that the government would put through a policy on which the people have given no decision, on whicli the people have not been consulted, and after the compact had been put through then the people would be consulted as to whether they liked it or not. That would be an entire reversal of the principle of responsible government as here set forth. The writer says further:
The real question decided by the vote at a general election is not whether certain members shall be elected or a certain government returned but what line of general policy or particular policy shall be followed, the decision being given by the individual voters at the polls according to their own views and interests.
Surely if that principle was right previous to 1908 it is the proper principle to follow now, to give the public an opportunity to express an opinion on this at a general election, the only time at which the people can have an opportunity to express an opinion. Further the writer says: Mr. EDWARDS
We cannot have successful responsible government without party, especially honest parties with whom principles are the end of party existence and not merely the means to party success. The evil of the party system is not in its use but in its abuse.
I commend that to the consideration of hon. gentlemen opposite, and ask that if the policy they are pursuing now is not rather a means to an end than a following of well known and definite principles.
One other paragraph in this pamphlet. Referring to the matter of the old fight in 1891 he says:
As Canada was entirely an exporter of natural products she clearly had the advantage, there was no hope of securing a renewal of the old treaty of 1851. The only possibility of securing free entrance of Canadian farm products into the United States was by giving free or preferred entrance to United States manufactures to Canadian markets.
That is the justification given for the course pursued in 1891 when the policy of the Liberal party was unrestricted reciprocity. Then it was set before the people that the only way in which we could get free entrance to the United States for natural products was to give a free entrance for American manufactured products to Canada. It seems to me that policy is now turned the other way round, and they are taking as the first step free trade in natural products to be followed by its logical conclusion, free trade in manufactured products.
We find the Liberal party following one course at one time and another course at another time, but each leading to the one end, namely, commercial union or free trade between Canada and the United States and the establishment of a common tariff on the North American continent against the rest of the world. It has been stated that if this compact goes into effect it will inure to the benefit of the farmers of Canada. If agricultural conditions in the United States are so much better than in Canada I ask any member of the government to tell me why it is that in the state of New York in the last ten years there have been 12,070 abandoned farms and
775,000	less acres of improved land; why is it that in Pennsylvania in the last ten years there have been 5,854 abandoned farms and 549,000 acres less of improved land in 1910 than in 1900; why it is that in the state of Ohio there have been 5,386 abandoned farms in the last ten years and 34,000 less acres of improved land in 1910 than in 1900; why is it that in the state of Vermont there were 506 abandoned farms in the last ten years and 494,000 less acres of improved land in 1910 than in 1900; why in New Hampshire there have been 2,411 abandoned farms in the last ten years and a decrease of 150,000 acres in the improved

acreage; why is it that in the state of Massachusetts in the last ten years there have been 1,203 abandoned farms and a decrease of 130,000 acres in improved acreage. Wlhy is it that in these six states just across the line there have been in the last ten years 27,380 abandoned farms and a decrease of the improved acreage amounting to 2,132,132 acres. These are official figures from the advance sheets issued by the Census Bureau at Washington and sent to me by Mr. Durand Chief Director of the United States Census Bureau. These are pertinent questions to ask those who argue that this reciprocity pact will advantage the Canadian farmer. Why is it that in the state of Massachussetts in 1909, 38 per cent of the farms were mortgaged and that in 1910, 41 per cent were mortgaged. And yet Massachusetts is alongside the Boston market so much vaunted by hon. gentlemen opposite, and it is within a few hours run o.f New York, Brooklyn, Pittsburg, Philadelphia and other large centres of population. Our people are being told in Ontario that if they had an opportunity of getting to the markets on the other side of the line the conditions in Canada would be similar to the conditions in the United States, but if the result of reciprocity is that they are to have in Canada conditions like those I have mentioned in the United States we don't want anything of this kind because conditions in Canada are infinitely better than they are on the other side of the line. And, yet, hon. gentlemen who advocate this pact offer no argument to answer such facts as I have presented. Do these gentlemen think it a fair deal to the farmers of this country to submit them to competition with people who have an advantage in climatic conditions? I can understand why people in certain parts of the world are in favour of free trade, but I cannot understand how any one truly interested in the prosperity of the Canadian farmer can advocate free trade. Under this pact the farmers of the Argentine Republic will be allowed to send their stufl into our market. The population of the Argentine is largely composed of Spanish, Italians and Indian natives and the labourer is paid 64 cents a day out of which he pays his board. The people of the Argentine do not have to build expensive houses nor buy fuel nor heavy clothing to protect themselves from cold, nor stables nor barns to protect their stock which run in the open during the entire year, nor, have they to maintain the high standard of civilization Canadians have, nor do they feel the responsibility of educating their children and beautifying their homes as we do. Nothing can be more unfair than to ask the farmers of Canada to compete with the farmers
of the Argentine and other countries similarly circumstanced. As to our wheat going to the American market, if it does go there the by-product of our wheat will go across the line also, and I would remind hon. gentlemen that the price of bran and shorts in Canada to-day is $6 and $7 a ton lower than in the United States, bran being quoted all through May and June in the United States, at from $29 to $30 a ton and white shorts at $34 a ton. If this pact goes through the Americans will have the benefit of the shorts and the farmers of Canada will have the shortage, and instead of the people of Ontario paying $23 and $24 a ton and the American $29 or $30 a ton the conditions will be reversed and the Canadian farmer will be paying the higher price. Add to that the advantage they have over us in the matter of climate and the abundance of corn which we cannot raise as they can, and give to them these advantages in the raising of cattle, and the farmers of Canada will be put out of business entirely.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-WINNER OF THE KING'S PRIZE AT BISLEY.
speechtext: I am not worrying about the farmers at all. So far as the section where I live is concerned, the farmers who understand this matter have absolutely no use for it whatever, and I have every confidence that if hon. gentlemen opposite would submit it to the farmers of this country, they would find that they would not endorse the position they take. The fact that they are not willing to submit it to the people is a clear evidence that they have not any confidence in the policy that they are advocating at the present time.
